    In a recent development, today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota. And while looking through their latest photos, I kept forgetting that I was looking at a garden in the Midwest! Arianne has shared their garden with us before, and I’m excited to see what they’ve been growing this year. Here’s Arianne:.

    It has been revealed that in Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden! It’s packed with flowers I start from seed—like zinnias, cosmos, statice, strawflower, celosia, and amaranth—along with overwintered dahlias. I love cutting fresh bouquets to gift to friends, family, and coworkers. When we’re not admiring the blooms, my husband is cooking outdoors—making wood-fired pizzas, wok dishes, and hosting family birthday celebrations right in the heart of our cozy yard.

    It has been revealed that arianne packs plenty of interest into the garden along in the front yard and along the curb strip. Plants in this section of the garden include dwarf purple smokebush, threadleaf bluestar (Amsonia hubrichtii, Zones 5–8), boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), lamb’s ear (Stachys byzantina, Zones 4–8), purpleleaf sand cherry (Prunus × cistena, Zones 2–8), coreopsis (Coreopsis cvs., Zones 3–9), alliums (Allium cvs., Zones 3–9), sedum, and artemisia. It’s a great mix of foliage colors and textures even when everything isn’t in bloom.

    Recent findings suggest that I love the placement of the patio and pathway. It’s a really useful design technique for maximizing every square inch of a small garden while still leaving plenty of room for outdoor living.

    Absolutely gorgeous section of the garden! This is where we really start to feel like we’re in the tropics. ‘Mars Madness’ hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus ‘Mars Madness’, Zones 4–9) has all the tropical drama while still being hardy enough for a Minneapolis winter. And it’s hard to miss those giant cannas and the colorful foliage on the coleus. I love all the red blooms too!

    According to recent reports, one of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual). So much of the color and interest here comes from foliage!

    According to recent reports, there is so much to look at in this section of the garden! Those variegated geranium leaves are striking, and I could go on and on about Arianne’s use of color and texture. The apple tree surrounded by all these ornamentals is an unexpected but lovely touch.

    Just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

    It has been revealed that another view of the backyard borders. There are so many plants packed into this garden, you would never believe this is a small urban backyard. And, if my eyes are working correctly, I’d say that’s a clover lawn?!

    In a recent development, tall conifers create a fantastic privacy screen in this view. The garden really is its own secluded paradise.

    A shady combination of hostas, ‘Banana Boat’ sedge (Carex siderosticha ‘Banana Boat’, Zones 4–9), painted fern, purple shield, coleus, and impatiens.

    Industry observers note that zinnias, statice, amaranth, and overwintered dahlias are just some of the blooms that make their way into bouquets for friends, family, and coworkers. So pretty!

    Thank you so much for sharing your garden with us again, Arianne! It’s always a treat to see what you and Micah are growing, and I think I could spend hours wandering around this garden and still find something upcoming to admire.

    Clean, Kink-Free Bends

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (382 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I wanted minisplits in my basement shop but was not looking forward to installing them because I knew running the lineset would be a circuitous affair.
    • I’ve always taken great pride in my plumbing and HVAC installations, and neatly run lines are characteristic of my perfectionist tendencies.
    • Recent findings suggest that while placing the order for my minisplits, I stumbled upon the EasyBend internal lineset bender.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I wanted minisplits in my basement shop but was not looking forward to installing them because I knew running the lineset would be a circuitous affair. Existing ductwork, radon piping, DWV piping, and my dust-­collection ductwork created several mechanical obstructions.

    I’ve always taken great pride in my plumbing and HVAC installations, and neatly run lines are characteristic of my perfectionist tendencies. In the past, I’ve used a ratcheting tubing bender to shape copper tubing and avoid kinks, but the insulation on pre-insulated minisplit linesets gets in the way and makes them difficult to work with.

    Recent findings suggest that while placing the order for my minisplits, I stumbled upon the EasyBend internal lineset bender. The EasyBend is a flexible plastic mandrel available in 13-ft. or 26-ft. lengths and 1/4-in., 3/8-in., 1/2-in., 5/8-in., and 3/4-in. diameters. To make a bend in the tubing, simply slide the mandrel into the tube at least 12 in. past the spot you intend to bend—no need to remove insulation from the tubing.

    Sources indicate that form the bend, then withdraw the mandrel. I used the EasyBend when installing my basement shop minisplit, and I was able to snake my linesets around all the obstructions and still have them neatly arranged, with no kinked copper.

    If you decide to try the Easy­Bend system, ream the pipe ends before inserting the mandrel. Otherwise, removal can be difficult and may damage the reusable tool. I also learned through experience that you need to withdraw the mandrel past your most recent bend, as it’s difficult to remove if you leave it in place through multiple bends.

    Recent findings suggest that to reduce the possibility of contamination, I pulled the EasyBend through a lint-free rag wrapped around the mandrel as I inserted it into the copper tubing. I also blew out the linesets with compressed nitrogen prior to making the connections.

    According to recent reports, I have since used EasyBend mandrels on other lineset installations and have been pleased with the results every time. A 13-ft. EasyBend mini­split kit with 1/4-in.- to 5/8-in.-dia. mandrels costs about $95 at SupplyHouse.com.

    In a recent development, — Arthur W. Henderson III, ER doctor and serial remodeler. Photos by Virginia Henderson.

    Self-Closing Dust Door

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (225 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that dust containment is critical on remodeling jobs.
    • Recently I decided to try the Re-U-Zip magnetic door.
    • I’ve found that the magnets have just the right amount of draw, making them easy to separate when walking through with an armful of tools or supplies but strong enough to close behind you.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that dust containment is critical on remodeling jobs. It only takes a little dust on a dining room table to sour a client’s impression of even the highest level of craftsmanship. The zipper door has long been the go-to option for getting in and out of temporary dust-containment setups, but torn zippers and snagged plastic can make them frustrating to use.

    Recently I decided to try the Re-U-Zip magnetic door. Instead of a zipper, the system uses a magnetic entry strip that attaches to peel-and-stick hook-and-loop backers adhered to the plastic barrier. When the job is done, the magnetic strip peels off for use on the next project.

    I’ve found that the magnets have just the right amount of draw, making them easy to separate when walking through with an armful of tools or supplies but strong enough to close behind you. One thing to note is that these doors don’t seal to the floor, so you’ll want to keep the work area under slightly negative pressure if possible.

    A kit with a 6-mil vinyl panel, one reusable magnetic entry strip, and four mounting strips cost about $85 at reuzip.com.

    Industry observers note that — Justin Fink, a restoration carpenter in Plainville, Conn. Photos courtesy of Re-U-Zip.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy. Nancy sent in photos of the trees and shrubs winding down the season in her garden, along with one of the last flowers still hanging on.

    This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

    My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.

    My paperbark maple (Acer griseum, Zones 4–8) has had a hard time coping with our summer droughts and water restrictions, but it looked a lovely red this fall.

    Recent findings suggest that this is another native tree that many people are not familiar with, fringe tree (Chionanthus virginicus, Zones 4–9), which has fragrant white flowers hanging from its branches in late spring to early summer. As you can see, it also looks beautiful in its yellow fall foliage.

    According to recent reports, in the front of this picture is a young sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua, Zones 5–9), which has spectacular red color in the fall and develops spiky seed balls as it matures. In the distance is a blackhaw viburnum (Viburnum prunifolium, Zones 3–9) showing its orange fall color.

    ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla (Fothergilla ‘Mount Airy’, Zones 5–8) glows red and orange in front of fragrant abelia (Abelia mosanensis, Zones 4–8), whose fall color is beginning to fade. The abelia will charm us all again in spring with its fragrant blooms.

    Sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus, Zones 5–9) on the right has turned a lovely yellow. Amazingly, all three sweetshrubs shown here had the bark eaten off around every trunk by rabbits last winter, killing every one. They all grew back from the roots, showing just how resilient they are. On the left, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla is showing off its red fall foliage, and in back is ‘Alice’ oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Alice’, Zones 5–9) with maroon fall foliage.

    One of the only flowers left blooming is ‘Sheffield Pink’ chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum ‘Sheffield Pink’, Zones 5–9), which complements the dark foliage of Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) behind it.

    Recent findings suggest that thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Nancy! Nancy states she’s ready to wander the garden, make her list of what needs dividing in spring, and figure out what latest plants need to be bought. Sounds like a good way to spend the off-season to me!

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re seeking a Technical Account Manager (TAM) to be the primary technical partner for our Team & customers after the sale, helping them adopt, operate, and get long-term value from Supabase.

    At Supabase, TAMs are the technical owners of their assigned accounts, working closely with our most valuable customers to:.

    Understand each customer’s architecture, use cases, constraints, and goals.

    Validate deployments and guide customers through onboarding and early success.

    Proactively surface risks and optimization opportunities before they become incidents.

    Coordinate internal teams on complex escalations and drive root cause analysis.

    Align Supabase capabilities with the customer’s roadmap.

    Recent findings suggest that successful TAMs are proactive, technically credible, and customer-first. TAM is a relationship, not a response channel: you’ll act as an extension of your customers’ teams and advocate on their behalf within Supabase.

    You’ll be joining our Success team, where you will be expected to lead and innovate around the following areas of responsibility:.

    Technical Ownership & Onboarding.

    Act as the technical owner for your assigned accounts, documenting environments, mapping dependencies, and tracking technical risks.

    Validate architecture and deployment plans after the sale, guide initial configuration and best practices, and make sure customers understand platform capabilities and limitations.

    Help customers reach early success milestones to shorten time to value and reduce early friction.

    Regularly review customer environments and usage patterns to identify scalability, performance, reliability, security, and compliance risks and opportunities.

    Blueprint upgrades and lifecycle events, and run architecture reviews for upcoming initiatives, including capacity and growth planning, feature readiness, and early identification of technical blockers.

    In a recent development, coordinate across Support and Engineering on complex or high-impact problems. TAMs are not frontline support, but provide the context, prioritization, and follow-through that drive resolution, root cause analysis, and preventative action.

    Serve as the voice of the customer to Engineering and Product, sharing specific, reproducible feedback on recurring pain points and taking part in beta and early access programs.

    Partner with Sales and Customer Success on account health and retention, with technical input on renewals, expansions, and evaluations, and early flags on risks to satisfaction.

    6+ years of relevant work experience in engineering, SRE, technical consulting, or similar, including operating production systems under real constraints.

    Strong technical depth across database internals, scalability, security posture, and infrastructure tradeoffs. You understand a customer’s architecture as well as they do, without escalating every question.

    A proactive mindset: you spot risks and optimization opportunities before the customer does, and you treat your accounts like a personal portfolio.

    Sound escalation judgment: you know when to escalate, when to resolve internally, and how to communicate clearly under pressure without creating noise.

    Very strong communication skills. TAMs explain complex issues to non-technical executives and root causes to senior engineers, often in the same day.

    Awareness of how TAM performance shows up in retention and NRR, including surfacing expansion signals and renewal risks early.

    Experience working in async or globally distributed teams.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    According to recent reports, supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

    According to recent reports, once a year, the entire company gathers in a fresh city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Industry observers note that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    In a recent development, we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    #147347. Breaking: If Walls Could Talk

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3642 w)

    Breaking: If Walls Could Talk

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3642 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Building science examines how heat, air, moisture, materials, and mechanical systems interact within buildings, with failures potentially causing comfort issues, moisture damage, poor indoor air quality, high energy bills, and reduced durability.
    • Recent findings suggest that building science focuses on how heat, air, moisture, materials, and mechanical systems interact inside a building.
    • It has been revealed that there’s a small but growing niche of tradespeople who specialize in diagnosing building-performance problems.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Building science examines how heat, air, moisture, materials, and mechanical systems interact within buildings, with failures potentially causing comfort issues, moisture damage, poor indoor air quality, high energy bills, and reduced durability. Building investigators use specialized tools to diagnose hidden defects and assess building performance by measuring factors such as temperature, humidity, air pressure, airflow, energy use, and concealed moisture. This article looks at seven of these tools: blower door, thermal-imaging camera, moisture meter, hygrometer, duct-leakage tester, digital manometer, and electricity monitor.

    Recent findings suggest that building science focuses on how heat, air, moisture, materials, and mechanical systems interact inside a building. When those systems aren’t working together properly, the results can include comfort complaints, moisture problems, poor indoor air quality, high energy use, or durability failures.

    It has been revealed that there’s a small but growing niche of tradespeople who specialize in diagnosing building-performance problems. Combining building-science knowledge with an understanding of how buildings are assembled, these professionals use specialized tools to uncover hidden defects, evaluate energy efficiency, and identify problems affecting comfort, durability, indoor air quality, and operating costs.

    I’ve spent much of the last decade investigating buildings with problems ranging from ice dams and moisture damage to comfort problems and unusually high energy bills. Rarely does the answer reveal itself with a visual-only inspection. More often the investigation involves gathering clues, testing theories, and using specialized tools to understand what the building is trying to tell us. In many ways, building investigators function like building doctors.

    Some of the tools used during investigations are familiar to most contractors, while others are highly specialized measuring instruments. Depending on the problem being investigated, they may measure temperature, humidity, pressure, airflow, energy use, or moisture hidden within building assemblies that cannot be identified through visual inspection alone.

    Industry observers note that this article covers many of the core tools used in building investigations, energy audits, and commissioning work. Though not a complete list, these are some of the instruments many experienced “building doctors” rely on to collect data and better understand how buildings perform.

    Recent findings suggest that before any investigation begins, safety comes first. Building investigators routinely carry wearable carbon monoxide monitors, combustible-gas detectors, and other personal safety equipment because they often enter homes without knowing the condition of the combustion appliances, venting systems, or gas piping. Understanding building performance is important, but first you need to know the building is safe to occupy. Then you can use these specialized tools to reveal what’s happening inside the building enclosure and mechanical systems.

    Doesn’t just measure leakage—it reveals how a building behaves as an air system.

    Sources indicate that A blower door is one of the most recognizable tools used in building diagnostics and commissioning. By temporarily pressurizing or depressurizing a building, investigators can measure how much air leaks through the building enclosure. The system typically consists of a calibrated fan mounted in an exterior doorway along with digital pressure gauges and software used to calculate leakage rates.

    Blower doors provide both quantitative and investigative information. In addition to measuring total building leakage, they can be combined with thermal-imaging cameras, smoke tools, or pressure diagnostics to help pinpoint where leaks are occurring. Many homes contain thousands of small leakage pathways—and occasionally larger holes—hidden around the enclosure. Modern software can estimate the energy penalty associated with excessive leakage based on climate, utility costs, and HVAC efficiency.

    Many assume that a blower door is only useful for measuring air leakage. In reality, much of its value comes from helping investigators understand how air moves through a building and how different assemblies are connected. Blower-door testing is great for diagnosing air-leakage problems, but sometimes it points to an entirely different concern. More than once I’ve tested older homes expecting to find significant air leakage, only to discover the house was relatively tight. In those cases, the blower door helped rule out air leakage as the primary problem and directed the investigation toward other causes of the comfort, moisture, or energy-use concerns—something I wouldn’t have known without testing.

    In a recent development, researchers and builders began paying much closer attention to air leakage in the late 1970s after recognizing how uncontrolled airflow affects energy use, comfort, indoor air quality, and moisture movement within assemblies. Air leakage can transport large amounts of moisture into walls, attics, and roof assemblies, sometimes creating hidden condensation and long-term durability problems. Code-required blower-door testing for latest homes became widespread with the 2012 edition of the International Residential Code, although the equipment had already been used in building research and energy auditing for decades.

    Operating a blower door is relatively straightforward, but interpreting the results requires training and experience. Organizations such as Building Performance Institute (BPI) and the Residential Energy Services Network (RESNET) offer courses that teach both testing procedures and building-science fundamentals. For contractors contemplating a blower-door purchase, the most important considerations are support, training, and compatibility with local programs or certification requirements.

    Industry observers note that two manufacturers dominate the residential blower-door market: Minneapolis Blower Door and Retrotec. Both use calibrated fans, digital manometers, adjustable frames, and nylon panels to measure building air leakage, and each is widely accepted for energy audits, code-compliance testing, and building investigations. Retrotec offers several fan/system configurations, while Minneapolis Blower Door just released its newest system, the Model 5.

    Provides powerful visual clues, but only when paired with building-science knowledge and verification.

    It has been revealed that thermal-imaging technology has improved dramatically over the past two decades. As performance has increased, prices have dropped, making thermal cameras far more accessible to builders, remodelers, and energy auditors. Better resolution, digital image overlay, multiple color palettes, and picture-in-picture displays have all made thermal images easier to interpret.

    Recent findings suggest that even with these advances, it’s important to understand what a thermal camera is showing. It doesn’t “see” air leaks, moisture, or missing insulation. It visualizes surface temperature differences within its field of view. In most cases, a temperature difference of about 10°F between indoors and outdoors is enough to produce useful images, though experienced people can often gather meaningful information with less by adjusting the camera’s settings.

    One of the most valuable uses for thermal imaging is in combination with a blower-door test. Depressurizing or pressurizing a house exaggerates leakage pathways, allowing the camera to reveal temperature patterns caused by moving air. Being able to see and document these leakage paths makes it much easier to diagnose problems and explain them to clients or crews.

    Industry observers note that thermal imaging has helped me locate everything from disconnected ductwork hidden above finished ceilings to wall cavities that were missed during insulation installation. Some common discoveries are air leaks around incomplete air barriers and unsealed wiring, plumbing, and framing penetrations between conditioned and unconditioned spaces.

    In a recent development, thermal imaging is also useful for finding compressed insulation, identifying active moisture problems, and spotting temperature anomalies in electrical or mechanical equipment. But interpretation requires caution. Reflective surfaces such as glass, polished metal, and foil-faced materials can create misleading images by reflecting infrared radiation rather than showing the actual surface temperature.

    Testo 860i smartphone thermal-imaging camera $500.

    Flir C5 compact thermal-imaging camera $700.

    The best way to learn thermal imaging is through hands-on training, where people can compare what the camera reveals with real-world conditions. That said, experience is the real teacher. The more images you capture—and verify through other diagnostic methods—the better your interpretation skills become. Online tutorials and manufacturer training resources can shorten the learning curve. Before purchasing a camera, consider that image resolution and thermal sensitivity often have a greater impact on usefulness than additional software features.

    Thermal-imaging cameras are available from several manufacturers, including FLIR, Fluke, Testo, and Seek. Performance varies significantly depending on image resolution, thermal sensitivity, field of view, and reporting capabilities. While entry-level cameras can identify obvious insulation deficiencies and air-leakage patterns, higher-resolution models often provide much more useful information during detailed investigations.

    Identifies what’s dry, what warrants ­monitoring, and what indicates risk.

    Water is one of the biggest threats to any structure. It finds ways into building assemblies through leaks, air movement, and vapor diffusion—and often remains hidden until visible damage appears. By the time paint peels, trim swells, or mold becomes visible, the problem may already be well advanced. Moisture meters help detect these challenges early, before they become expensive repairs.

    Recent findings suggest that the two most common types of moisture meters are pin and pinless. A pin-type meter uses two sharp probes inserted into the material being tested. The meter measures electrical resistance between the pins and converts that reading into moisture content. Because different materials conduct electricity differently, settings often need to be adjusted depending on the building material being tested.

    Industry observers note that pinless meters work by sending an electromagnetic signal into the material without puncturing the surface. This allows for quick scanning across large areas without leaving pinholes. Pinless meters are useful for locating suspicious areas before confirming readings with a pin meter. However, pinless meters can be affected by metal fasteners, wiring, metal framing or ductwork, foil-faced insulation, and some roofing materials, all of which can create false readings.

    When taking moisture readings, I often begin with a pinless meter to quickly scan a large area without damaging finishes. Then if I find an elevated reading, I verify using a pin meter before drawing conclusions. More than once, that second step has prevented me from chasing a false positive caused by hidden metal or other materials behind the surface.

    In a recent development, one place I frequently use a moisture meter is along the interior side of roof eaves. Wind-washing through fibrous insulation can create temperature patterns that look very similar to moisture problems on a thermal image. A quick scan with a pinless moisture meter can confirm whether moisture is actually present or if the matter is related to air movement and insulation performance instead.

    For wood framing, moisture content below about 15% is generally considered dry. Readings above 20% deserve attention, as sustained moisture levels in that range can create conditions favorable for mold growth and decay. Finish materials such as hardwood flooring often require much tighter moisture tolerances to avoid movement, cupping, or other failures.

    Like most diagnostic tools, moisture meters are most effective when paired with context. Elevated readings don’t always indicate an active leak. They may reflect seasonal humidity changes, recently wetted materials, or temperature-related measurement variations.

    Training requirements for moisture meters are relatively minimal, but understanding what constitutes a normal moisture content for a given material is just as crucial as understanding how to operate the meter itself. Good interpretation requires understanding the assembly being tested and confirming findings through visual inspection or additional testing.

    It has been revealed that delmhorst, Tramex, and Lignomat are among the most recognized manufacturers of moisture meters used in building investigations. Most investigators eventually find themselves using both pin and pinless meters. Pinless meters are excellent for promptly scanning large areas without damaging finishes, while pin meters are often used to verify suspicious readings and obtain measurements that are more precise.

    Reveals current conditions and long-term trends in temperature and humidity.

    Temperature, humidity, and dew point all play a major role in building performance. Together they influence indoor air quality, comfort, condensation risk, and the long-term durability of building materials. Relative humidity describes how much moisture the air contains compared to the maximum amount it could hold at that temperature. Because warm air can hold more moisture than cold air, relative humidity changes as temperature changes. This relationship becomes important when evaluating dew point—the temperature at which air can no longer hold its moisture, causing water vapor to condense into liquid water.

    SensorPush G1 WiFi Gateway ($100) and HT.w ($70) data-logging hygrometer.

    According to recent reports, HOBO MX1101 data-logging hygrometer $165. Photo courtesy of HOBO.

    Sources indicate that many building failures begin when warm, moisture-laden air encounters a cold surface. If that surface is at or below the dew point, condensation can form inside wall cavities, on window glass, or within other vulnerable parts of the enclosure.

    Sources indicate that most hygrometers combine humidity and temperature sensors into a single device, and many modern models can log data over time while transmitting readings through Bluetooth or Wi-Fi. This allows users to monitor conditions remotely and identify patterns that would otherwise be missed during a short inspection.

    Hygrometers with data-logging capabilities are particularly valuable because many moisture-related concerns are intermittent. A crawlspace may perform well during one visit but experience elevated humidity during seasonal transitions or heavy rain events. An attic may remain dry most of the winter but reach condensation conditions during a brief change in temperature. Continuous monitoring helps reveal these trends.

    Sauerman Si-HH3 hygrometer $185.

    According to recent reports, during one investigation, I left temperature and humidity loggers in a guest cabin after the homeowner reported recurring mold growth on interior surfaces. Conditions appeared normal during my visit, but several weeks of data revealed short periods when indoor humidity spiked while the cabin was occupied. Whatever the guests were doing—cooking, showering—was enough to push humidity levels into a range that supported mold growth. Without the data loggers, the cause of the problem likely would have remained undiagnosed.

    When selecting a monitoring system, focus on accuracy, data-storage capabilities, battery life, and ease of exporting data.

    It has been revealed that manufacturers such as SensorPush and Onset (HOBO) produce hygrometers capable of measuring temperature, humidity, and dew-point conditions. Less expensive monitors may be perfectly adequate for occasional spot checks, while professional-grade tools typically offer tighter, more robust reporting features.

    Demonstrates how duct tightness affects not only energy use but also airflow, comfort, and durability.

    Duct-leakage testing uses a calibrated fan—called a duct tester or duct blaster—to pressurize or depressurize the duct system and measure how much air escapes through leaks. Similar in concept to a blower-door test, the process provides a quantitative measurement of duct leakage.

    In a recent development, duct leakage is not simply an energy problem. Leakage can affect pressure relationships, comfort, humidity control, and indoor air quality. Even when ductwork is fully inside the conditioned enclosure, air leaking from the system means that conditioned air is not being delivered at the rate for which it was designed. That can create room-to-room comfort imbalances, reduce system efficiency, and complicate airflow balancing. This is one reason why duct-leakage testing has become increasingly important in modern energy codes. Beyond identifying performance problems, duct testing is also useful for verifying installation quality.

    According to recent reports, current code requirements recognize that duct leakage affects system performance regardless of where the ductwork is located. But when ducts run outside the building enclosure—in vented attics, crawlspaces, or garages—the consequences become much more serious. Leakage can create pressure imbalances that drive unintended air movement through the building enclosure. The house may become pressurized or depressurized, leading to increased air infiltration, humidity problems, comfort complaints, and indoor air quality concerns.

    Recent findings suggest that consider a common example: leaky supply ducts located in a vented attic in a hot, humid climate. Conditioned air escapes into the attic, resulting in an immediate energy loss. At the same time, the loss of supply air depressurizes the house. That negative pressure pulls hot, humid outdoor air into the living space through leaks in the enclosure, increasing both sensible and latent cooling loads. The result is a double energy penalty, along with increased moisture risk and reduced occupant comfort. The only way to know how much leakage is occurring is to test. As an added benefit, a duct-testing system can often double as a blower door for testing smaller or exceptionally tight structures.

    Minneapolis Duct Blaster $3990. Photos by Randy Williams.

    For contractors already performing blower-door testing, duct-leakage testing is a natural extension. Training is available through BPI, RESNET, HVAC organizations, and the manufacturers themselves.

    The residential duct-testing market is largely represented by Minneapolis Blower Door’s Duct Blaster and Retrotec’s DucTester systems. Both use calibrated fans and digital manometers to quantify duct leakage and are widely employed for code compliance, commissioning, and troubleshooting HVAC performance problems.

    Reveals invisible pressure relationships that drive air movement through buildings.

    Sources indicate that air moves from areas of higher pressure to areas of lower pressure. A digital manometer measures those pressure differences, helping investigators understand why air is moving through a building and where problems may be occurring.

    A digital manometer is one of the most versatile tools in building diagnostics. It serves as the “brain” behind blower-door and duct-leakage testing, but its usefulness extends far beyond those applications.

    While blower doors often get most of the attention, the digital manometer is often the tool doing the real analytical work behind the scenes. Digital manometers are commonly used to measure duct static pressure, evaluate total building pressure, and perform zonal pressure diagnostics. One important application is combustion appliance zone (CAZ) testing.

    In homes with atmospherically vented combustion appliances, excessive negative pressure can cause combustion gases to spill back into the living space rather than vent outdoors. A manometer can help an investigator diagnose these pressure imbalances before they become safety hazards.

    Sources indicate that manometers are also used to check pressure differences between bedrooms and the main living area. Closed bedroom doors combined with inadequate return-air pathways can create pressure imbalances that affect comfort and air distribution throughout the home.

    Industry observers note that manometers can also reveal how strongly an attached garage is connected to the living space, or whether an attic is unintentionally communicating with conditioned areas. In addition, manometers can be used with other diagnostic tools, including pressure pans, exhaust-fan flow meters, and products such as the Digital TrueFlow Grid, which is employed to measure HVAC system airflow.

    It has been revealed that while digital manometers are relatively easy to operate, pressure diagnostics can take some practice. Training through BPI, RESNET, and manufacturer-sponsored courses can help owners develop the skills needed to interpret pressure relationships within buildings.

    In a recent development, A common frustration for upcoming manometer users is incorrect tubing connections, which can produce confusing readings. Developing a habit of checking hose locations and understanding reference pressures can eliminate many troubleshooting headaches.

    Many building-performance tests rely on digital manometers to measure pressure differences and airflow. Commonly used instruments include The Energy Conservatory’s DG-1000 and DG-8 as well as Retrotec’s DM32X and Solo series.

    Identifies hidden energy loads and patterns of consumption.

    Sources indicate that not every building-performance problem involves air leakage, moisture, or comfort complaints. Sometimes the glitch is simply electric equipment operating when it shouldn’t be.

    Recent findings suggest that an electric crawlspace heater running continuously or a well pump stuck in constant operation can quietly add more than a hundred dollars to a monthly utility bill. I’ve diagnosed both problems recently using a clamp-on ammeter, which measures electrical current. In each case, identifying the unexpected electrical load solved the mystery much faster than inspecting insulation levels or mechanical equipment.

    Industry observers note that investigators often use a clamp-on ammeter to measure current draw directly at the electrical service panel. By checking the main service conductors and then isolating individual branch circuits, it is often possible to identify unexpected electrical loads.

    Because this work is performed inside energized electrical equipment, it should only be done by trained professionals familiar with electrical safety procedures. Not all building investigators have the training needed to safely perform panel-level electrical diagnostics, and in some cases an electrician may be needed.

    In a recent development, for plug-in appliances, a simple watt meter can provide immediate insight into electrical use. Unlike panel-level electrical diagnostics with a clamp-on ammeter, watt meters do not require specialized electrical training and can be used safely by most building investigators and homeowners when evaluating plug-in equipment.

    Sources indicate that these devices plug into a standard receptacle, with the appliance connected through the meter to display real-time power consumption. Many can also log usage over time to reveal longer-term patterns.

    It has been revealed that for electrical investigations, clamp-on ammeters from manufacturers such as Fluke and Klein are commonly used to measure current draw within electrical systems. Plug-in watt meters, such as the Kill A Watt, provide a simple and accessible way to evaluate the energy use of individual appliances and equipment without the need for panel-level electrical diagnostics.

    One of the most frequently used tools in building diagnostics is something nearly everyone already carries—a cell phone.

    Photographs of equipment nameplates, hidden conditions inside attics and crawlspaces, unusual assembly details, or visible failures often become crucial references later in an investigation. Photos and videos can also help explain findings to homeowners, making invisible or hard-to-access problems easier to understand. A quick product lookup, a manufacturer specification search, or even a phone call to a colleague can sometimes provide the missing piece needed to solve a diagnostic mystery.

    In a recent development, like every diagnostic tool, a phone is only as valuable as the person using it. Technology continues to improve, making diagnostic tools more capable and accessible than ever before. But no tool diagnoses a building on its own. The most valuable part of any investigation remains the person holding the instrument—the ability to observe, ask questions, interpret data, and connect seemingly unrelated clues. In building investigations, observation and critical thinking remain the most important tools of all.

    In a recent development, — Green Building Advisor editor Randy Williams specializes in energy audits and residential building diagnostics. Photos by Brian Pontolilo, except where noted.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, in this article, tech editor Mark Petersen discusses some aspects of deck building that may not be addressed by the building code or caught during a deck permit proposal review or site inspection.
    • Industry observers note that I’ve built a lot of decks, some still standing after 30-plus years.
    • On the flip side, I’ve come across structures that range from somewhat wobbly to absolutely unsafe due to feeble footings, poorly installed or absent ledger flashing, undersized framing, and missing or misused hardware and fasteners.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, in this article, tech editor Mark Petersen discusses some aspects of deck building that may not be addressed by the building code or caught during a deck permit proposal review or site inspection. He focuses on building secure footings, ensuring proper ledger fastening, avoiding flashing mistakes, using correct connectors, and strengthening the framing.

    Industry observers note that I’ve built a lot of decks, some still standing after 30-plus years. I’ve also worked with several deck-building rock stars to create articles on the subject. I’ve even helped companies like Trex create a bunch of how-to content. In all my years of research and hands-on experience, I’ve seen plenty of examples of decks built to last.

    On the flip side, I’ve come across structures that range from somewhat wobbly to absolutely unsafe due to feeble footings, poorly installed or absent ledger flashing, undersized framing, and missing or misused hardware and fasteners.

    Building to code and following the requirements spelled out by your local building department will get you most of the way to a safe and durable deck, but even a code-compliant deck can be improved with some due diligence and attention to detail.

    In this article, I’ve focused on some vulnerabilities that may not be addressed by the building code or caught during a deck permit strategy review or site inspection. Think of this as an above-and-beyond checklist of details worth considering on your next deck build..

    In a recent development, drawing by Christopher Mills. Click here to enlarge.

    For years I worked for a production builder. They used to insulate a home’s rim-joist cavity with batt insulation and no vapor retarder, which was code-approved at the time. This caused all sorts of moisture damage from water vapor that was driven through the cavity.

    According to recent reports, instead of switching to rigid or spray foam, their first fix was to install SIP rim joists, the most common of which have a core of EPS insulation sandwiched between OSB sheathing. This solution lasted less than a year because uninformed deck builders and homeowners assumed they could use standard lag screws to then attach deck ledgers to the rim joist.

    The result was that most of those fasteners were secured to only the two layers of plywood that made up the SIP, rather than solid-sawn lumber—a serious problem when the connection is responsible for supporting the deck.

    According to recent reports, so, don’t assume there’s a conventional solid-sawn rim joist behind the sheathing. The floor system might include an SIP rim joist or floor trusses with just a ribbon board instead of a solid ledger. When building a latest deck, a permit blueprint review or site inspection will hopefully catch this, but if you are resurfacing an existing deck, now is the time to confirm a solid ledger connection.

    If you discover an SIP rim joist or a floor system that can’t support a conventional ledger connection, try to track down the manufacturer of the components in question for an approved attachment solution. If that’s not an option, you could consult an engineer or add a beam and posts near the house and build the deck as a freestanding structure.

    Don’t attach a deck ledger to the rim joist of a cantilevered bump-out or bay window, or directly to a stud wall.

    Neither provides the load path assumed by conventional prescriptive ledger details. Nevertheless, this was common practice back in the day.

    In fact, the ledger on my own son’s house is attached to a bay. A site inspection will likely catch this code violation, but if you are just making cosmetic improvements that don’t require a permit, do your due diligence.

    In some cases, these connections can be made to work, but they typically require an engineered design and structural modifications, which might involve tearing into a finished ceiling to add blocking or other framing reinforcement. As with any questionable ledger connection, the simpler solution is to treat the deck as freestanding.

    Add a beam and posts close to the house so the deck loads are carried directly to footings rather than relying on a questionable ledger connection. That’s the fix I plan to make on my son’s house. In the meantime, I warned him against throwing any parties on the deck.

    Sources indicate that in my work as a contractor, I replaced several patio doors after either the door sill or ledger flashing failed, allowing water to rot the subfloor and some of the framing below it. I came across this problem primarily when deck boards were installed right up under the door sill, where splashing rain and melting Minnesota snow combined to wreak havoc over the years. To help prevent this, whenever possible I would install the deck a few inches below the door sill. I also instructed my customers to keep snow from piling up against the door.

    Recent findings suggest that the main hurdle to installing a deck below the door sill is maintaining proper ledger-fastener placement. On a large deck, the ledger may be as deep as the house rim joist and dropping it a few inches can make it impossible to meet the required fastener edge distances in both the ledger and the rim joist. One solution is to use smaller deck joists and reduce their span by adding another beam. If this doesn’t work, you may need to consult an engineer for an alternative connection detail.

    Of course, lowering the deck surface below the door sill isn’t as much of a concern in warm, dry regions—and it isn’t always an option when someone in the house has mobility challenges.

    Drawing by Christopher Mills. Click here to enlarge.

    Industry observers note that the only deck callback I ever received happened after the first time I worked with composite fascia boards. I didn’t use enough fasteners. I thought the manufacturer’s recommended screw spacing was preposterous overkill, but I was wrong. The fascia buckled, and I returned to the scene, tail between my legs, to add more screws.

    Recent findings suggest that in addition to protecting your reputation, following manufacturer recommendations can also preserve warranties. If you use unapproved fasteners or hidden clips on composite decking and there’s a factory defect, some companies might not stand behind their product. Most factory warranties stipulate using only approved installation methods and materials.

    It has been revealed that double-check that the structural hardware you grab is rated for exterior use with the treated lumber you’re using. I nearly walked out of a home center with interior-grade joist hangers that were in the wrong bin. They looked almost identical to the exterior versions. Also, don’t mix stainless-steel and galvanized connectors and fasteners; dissimilar metals can accelerate corrosion.

    Just as important, use the fasteners specified by the connector manufacturer. Short hanger nails, roofing nails, deck screws, and whatever happens to be in your tool pouch aren’t necessarily acceptable substitutes. Pay particular attention to double-shear hangers: The angled fasteners often need to be longer than the face nails so they penetrate through the joist and well into the supporting member. And fill the required holes—structural hardware only provides its rated capacity when it’s installed the way it was tested.

    For comprehensive info on deck hardware, including fastener and hardware options and how each connection works to keep the deck structure intact, check out Mike Guertin’s video series, “Critical Deck-Framing Connections.”.

    Drawing by Christopher Mills. Click here to enlarge.

    Drawing by Christopher Mills. Click here to enlarge.

    — Mark Petersen is tech editor. Drawings by Christopher Mills.

    Industry observers note that bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall. While the trees certainly put on a show, Bonnie says the shrubs were the real stars this year. Here’s Bonnie:.

    According to recent reports, colorado put on a spectacular fall color display this year. My garden was filled with so many vivid hues that I had to capture them in photos. Some years are more colorful than others, and this was certainly a good one! The standout colors came not from the trees, but from the shrubs.

    Sources indicate that welcome to my fall garden! Just walk through the arch and see the colors beyond. ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) starts in spring with dark burgundy leaves, turns green by late summer, and finishes the season in bright yellow. I love this tree!

    Industry observers note that other stars in my fall garden are the barberries, hydrangeas, dwarf smokebushes (Cotinus coggygria cvs., Zones 4–8), and spireas. Oh, and the Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) in the back turned a lovely red this year.

    Barberry, dwarf smokebush, and spireas in the back make a nice composition.

    Industry observers note that I’m in love with these ‘Annabelle’ smooth hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens ‘Annabelle’, Zones 3–9). They are all over my yard.

    Another hydrangea vignette with viburnum, boxwood, and Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra, Zones 5–9) in front.

    I love the beautiful colors of this barberry.

    Around the other side of our yard, the dwarf smokebush shines among the evergreens and the orange leaves of the mountain ash and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos, Zones 3–8) trees.

    Looking toward the front yard, the dwarf smokebush steals the show!

    Another view from the front yard.

    A weeping Norway spruce (Picea abies, Zones 3–7) and barberry make a beautiful combination.

    Industry observers note that thanks for sharing your beautiful fall garden with us, Bonnie! The trees are gorgeous, but I agree that the shrubs really stole the show this year.

    #147339. Breaking: Keep Ducts Where They Belong

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2454 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finehomebuilding ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Keep Ducts Where They Belong

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2454 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that installing HVAC equipment and ductwork in unconditioned attics can increase energy costs, reduce comfort, and contribute to air leakage, condensation, mold growth, and indoor air quality problems.
    • For decades, houses have been built with forced-air ductwork and heating and cooling equipment in unconditioned attics.
    • My manufacturer, Aarow Building, has been building high-performance homes in Missouri for going on three decades now.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that installing HVAC equipment and ductwork in unconditioned attics can increase energy costs, reduce comfort, and contribute to air leakage, condensation, mold growth, and indoor air quality problems. Plenum trusses create dedicated spaces above ceilings for ductwork and other mechanical systems within the home’s conditioned envelope, helping maintain consistent ceiling heights while improving energy efficiency and durability. Successful implementation requires early coordination among builders, architects, HVAC designers, and truss manufacturers, along with carefully planned duct layouts and continuous, airtight control layers to prevent moisture problems and ensure long-term performance.

    For decades, houses have been built with forced-air ductwork and heating and cooling equipment in unconditioned attics. The wide-open, easy-to-access attic space makes the practice common, convenient, and familiar for the framing and mechanical trades. But from a building-performance standpoint, it’s a terrible idea. Vented attics are extremely hot in summer and cold in winter, so every foot of duct placed in that location exposes the conditioned air within the ductwork to temperatures way beyond those inside the house.

    My manufacturer, Aarow Building, has been building high-performance homes in Missouri for going on three decades now. We have a hot, humid climate and—like in many places—attic ductwork is common here, so we’ve seen plenty of examples of what can happen when you install HVAC equipment in an unconditioned space.

    For starters, the extreme temperature difference between the conditioned air inside the ducts and the temperature outside them results in a house that uses more energy and is more expensive to heat and cool compared to a house with an HVAC system inside the conditioned space. And the additional expense isn’t limited to operational costs. HVAC ducts and equipment in unconditioned spaces must have higher capacities to compensate for the adverse conditions where they’re located, meaning the systems are more expensive.

    Higher costs are not the only downsides. Supply and return air leaks are common with HVAC systems in attics and are problematic from a building-durability and performance perspective. Supply leaks waste conditioned air and pressurize the attic, which depressurizes the house, causing additional air leakage in the conditioned space—and in extreme scenarios, backdrafting of combustion appliances.

    Recent findings suggest that backdrafting can release carbon monoxide into the home, creating a serious risk of poisoning. There’s also a lot of water vapor in flue gasses, which can create humidity problems and mold growth. Equally common are return leaks that pull dusty, humid, or hot attic air into the heating or cooling system, negatively affecting energy efficiency, occupant comfort, and indoor air quality.

    It has been revealed that air-conditioning supply ducts, which are cold, often become condensing surfaces. Condensing water can ruin finishes and lead to mold growth that may or may not be visible. Mold you can’t see can be especially problematic for sensitive individuals who might experience cold-like symptoms, asthma, or other respiratory problems. Similar problems can occur in cold climates when warm, conditioned air contacts cold spaces, creating condensation and potential mold problems. Even the most reliable HVAC system, when located outside the enclosure, can lead to comfort complaints and callbacks that are hard to diagnose and fix.

    According to recent reports, you can avoid all these problems by making room for HVAC ducts inside the house’s conditioned space during the design phase, before the house is built. The concept is not newly introduced—building scientists started advocating for ductwork within conditioned spaces in the late ’80s and early ’90s, and conscientious builders and designers paid attention. They developed methods for hiding ductwork in dropped hallway ceilings and in soffits that run along the tops of walls (see the drawings).

    Industry observers note that these methods work—but from a design perspective, employing them can be tough on some homes. I’ve found that soffits in bedrooms are almost always unwanted by designers and clients. I think the best way to hide ducts, both major and small, is to place them in ceiling chases using plenum trusses.

    My first exposure to plenum trusses came from architect Steve Baczek. For a period, Steve was working with a production builder in the Southwest United States that offered a comfort guarantee for every home they built. One of the ways they ensured comfort was by keeping the HVAC system inside the building envelope. In some parts of the house, Steve hid ductwork in soffits, but he also used plenum trusses in places where soffits were impractical. The idea of using plenum trusses stuck with me.

    We eventually began using plenum trusses in some of our builds for the same reasons as Steve: greater comfort, efficiency, and building durability. In 2017, our company made the decision that ductwork and HVAC equipment would be installed inside the conditioned enclosure whenever possible. In homes with a conditioned attic, the solution is easy. The ducts can simply live in the attic. The same is true when we have a conditioned crawlspace or basement available for distribution.

    According to recent reports, many of the homes we build, however, are slab-on-grade with a vented attic above them. Those homes require another strategy, and plenum trusses have become one of our preferred solutions. They allow us to maintain consistent ceiling heights throughout the house while still providing a dedicated space for ductwork and other mechanical systems inside the building envelope. The result gives us the architectural appearance we want without compromising the mechanical strategy, occupant comfort, or energy efficiency.

    Plenum trusses are engineered with an open space free of chords and braces that becomes a cavity for ducts, pipes, and refrigeration lines running perpendicular to the trusses. This plenum cavity is lined with an air-impermeable material, typically wood sheathing or drywall for airtightness. Ducts can also be run in angled plenums or in an airtight plenum space made between two trusses, as seen in the photos below.

    It has been revealed that parallel Plenum: In this space, eight girder trusses have an opening that allows a duct to pass through them and then turn 90° into a plenum space built on-site from taped sheathing between two of the girder trusses. Both site-built and engineered plenum spaces need a continuous air barrier—in this case, taped sheathing—to prevent air movement through the plenum space.

    Angled Plenum: To get the conditioned air to its intended registers most efficiently, the main plenum on this project is angled and installed within 10 individually engineered trusses. Each truss has the plenum space offset a few inches from the previous truss’s plenum space, creating the angled plenum. It took about an hour with the truss designer to plan this layout.

    Strapped Ceiling: Once the ductwork is installed and sealed and other mechanicals are in place, the ceiling is strapped with 2×4 furring for securing the finished drywall ceiling.

    A plenum truss offers a way to design a house’s framing around the mechanical systems, rather than squeezing ductwork into whatever leftover space is available. In simple terms, the bottom chord of a plenum truss is notched with a framed rectangle above, creating a dedicated service cavity, or chase, above the finished ceiling. Importantly, the chase is within the building enclosure, beneath the air, insulation, and vapor control layers—unlike an unconditioned attic, which is essentially outside the building. In addition to ductwork, the plenum space can also house electrical and low-voltage wiring, pipes, and other mechanical systems while keeping them inside the conditioned space of the home.

    It has been revealed that the important point is that the chase is designed, not discovered. You can’t build the chase with field alterations after the trusses arrive. By then, the rooflines, heel heights, load paths, bearing points, ceiling planes, and mechanical layout are already largely locked in. A plenum-truss strategy can only work when the builder, architect, mechanical designer, and truss supplier are involved early on and work together. In my experience, the biggest challenge has been the truss design. Nearly every builder or designer I know who uses plenum trusses has encountered some degree of resistance or hesitation from a truss manufacturer, which I think is understandable. We are asking the truss designer to create something more complicated than a conventional roof truss while accommodating structural loads, duct dimensions, roof geometry, bearing locations, and the other constraints of the building.

    According to recent reports, the best results we have had come from working directly with the truss designer early in the process. Whenever possible, we sit down with the designer and work through the layout before the trusses are finalized. An extra hour spent with a truss designer is how you end up with a plenum large enough to fit and efficiently route the ducts while framing the complicated rooflines typical of the custom homes we build. Modern truss-design software makes it relatively easy to look at the proposed truss geometry and determine if the plenum will be significant enough and correctly positioned for efficiently routing ducts that are the right size.

    Plenum ceilings use furred-down framing or drywall-suspension systems to lower the entire ceiling. The system requires a second air barrier above the furred-down section(s), adding significant cost and complexity to the whole ceiling assembly and not just the plenum service cavity.

    Lowered ceilings refer to a section of lowered ceiling (often in hallways), and were pioneered by building scientists as a way to keep ductwork in the conditioned space. The system is less expensive than dropping an entire ceiling, but many clients find the lowered portion of ceiling makes the hallway or other space feel oppressive or confining.

    Wall-to-ceiling soffits provide a space between the ceiling and the top of built-in cabinetry. Unfortunately, the design is often limited to concealing small ducts, and clients and designers often object to soffits outside the kitchen, especially when they obstruct a view or look like an afterthought.

    Sources indicate that conditioned attics bring the insulation, air-control, and vapor-control layers to the roof sheathing, typically with spray foam on the underside of the roof sheathing. But insulating an entire attic with spray foam is expensive, and conditioned attics add a lot of space that must be temperature-controlled, increasing costs over time.

    It has been revealed that once the house design is finalized, the next step is to determine where the ducts and equipment need to go. That means the HVAC design must be figured out before the trusses are ordered. The air-handler location, trunk lines, branch runs, register locations, return ducts, and grilles need to be finalized during the design process. A real duct layout matters. A rectangular box on a plan marked “mechanical” is not enough, so we engage our mechanical design team early in the process and make sure the duct size and routing is specified in their HVAC design. Leaving the duct sizing and routing to whoever shows up on installation day is never the right approach.

    Industry observers note that once the duct layout is understood, the truss designer can design the truss framing to accommodate it. The chase needs to be deep and wide enough for the ductwork and anything else other trades require in the plenum space. It also needs to provide reasonable access for the people doing the work. If a duct must be bent, crushed, or forced around a framing member, the truss and/or HVAC design has failed. This is where builders need to be assertive in preconstruction. It’s not enough to simply ask whether the ductwork will fit—the HVAC designers should be able to identify on the prepares where it will fit. By the end of the design process, the framing proposal, mechanical plan, and truss drawings must agree with one another.

    Recent findings suggest that A plenum truss only improves building and HVAC performance if the service cavity is within the home’s conditioned enclosure, without any gaps in the control layers. The air-barrier location has to be clear, which can be verified using what building scientist Joe Lstiburek and architect Steve Baczek describe as the “red pen test.” You should be able to trace the home’s entire air barrier location on the plans without lifting a red pen. If the ceiling drywall is the primary air barrier and vapor-control layer, then the plenum needs to be detailed so the ceiling drywall connects to the drywall or sheathing surrounding the plenum cavity, keeping the air- and vapor-control layers continuous. In most cases, this means the plenum is drywalled inside, ducts are installed and sealed, and then ceiling drywall is installed below the plenum, creating a flat ceiling with hidden ductwork above.

    According to recent reports, we use Zip System sheathing as our air control layer in the plenum space and on the rest of the building enclosure. Our framing crews install and tape the sheathing in the plenum space as part of their framing contract. The material might cost a little more than a drywall air barrier, but we find that having the framers install the air barrier works better with job sequencing than having the drywallers at the project twice, first to install and tape the plenum drywall and a second time to drywall the rest of the house. Whether you use drywall or taped sheathing, the takeaway is the same: All three sides (sides and cap) of the plenum, and where it meets the ceiling drywall, must be airtight.

    The enclosure must also be airtight for vapor control, as most water that condenses on building surfaces and in cavities leading to mold and damage is the result of water vapor carried by air leaks that condenses on cold surfaces. Condensation can occur if the plenum space is not properly sealed from air movement, so you need a continuous air control layer in the plenum space and throughout the rest of the building for effective air and vapor control.

    Sources indicate that there’s no question that plenum trusses require more preconstruction planning than installing ducts and air handlers in unvented attics, and they typically add to the cost of a truss package. But the upfront planning and additional costs should be weighed against the cost of comfort complaints, wasted energy dollars, mold risk, and the labor involved with sealing penetrations and insulating ducts and HVAC equipment in unvented attics. Keeping ducts and HVAC equipment out of unconditioned spaces makes longer-lasting, more comfortable houses, which makes the additional effort and expense a smart investment for our clients.

    It has been revealed that — Jake Bruton is the president of Aarow Builders in Columbia, Mo. Photos by the author. Drawings by Dan Thornton.

    Fiber-Cement Plank Repair

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that I need to remove 12 courses of blind-nailed 5-1/4-in.-wide fiber-cement lap siding with a 4-in.
    • It’s challenging to remove blind-nailed fiber-cement lap siding, but patience and an extra set of hands make removing and reinstalling the planks easier.
    • First, mark out the damaged area with painter’s tape.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that I need to remove 12 courses of blind-nailed 5-1/4-in.-wide fiber-cement lap siding with a 4-in. exposure to repair a 5-ft. by 5-ft. section of wall behind it. I’d like to reinstall the old siding without it looking like a repair. What’s the best way to remove fiber-cement lap siding without damaging the planks? How can I make removal and reinstallation less noticeable?

    It’s challenging to remove blind-nailed fiber-cement lap siding, but patience and an extra set of hands make removing and reinstalling the planks easier.

    First, mark out the damaged area with painter’s tape. You’ll have to remove full pieces of siding for the repair, so look for the nearest butt joints between individual planks to the left and right of the taped area. Mark the joints in every course of the taped repair area. Plank joints are generally staggered by two studs in successive courses—32 in. or 48 in., depending on the stud spacing. If you’re lucky, the repair area will fit within one 12-ft. plank, so you’ll need to remove just one plank per course between the nearest joints. More likely, you’ll need to remove two. This takes more time, but the removal process is the same.

    According to recent reports, the first plank is the hardest to remove. Start with the uppermost course in the area you marked out and gently pry up the overlying plank far enough to locate the nails. Then mark the nail locations with small pieces of tape on the overlying course. The butt joints to the left and right of the plank may have been caulked. If so, carefully cut through the sealant with a utility knife.

    Recent findings suggest that when fiber-cement planks are 8 in. or wider, you can lift the bottom edge far enough to pry out the nails from the plank below by slipping a thin flat bar under that plank and up to the shank of the nail. Gently pry the plank up slightly and then remove the flat bar. Press down on the top edge of the plank so the nail head stands proud of the surface, then set the flat bar under the nail head and pry it out.

    Recent findings suggest that prying up narrower planks to pull 2-in. or longer nails often breaks the plank, so in these situations I use a thin cutting tool to cut the nails holding the plank—the Malco Hidden Nail Cutter is made for this job, though you can also use a reciprocating saw with a long metal-cutting blade. Set a 1-ft.-sq. piece of PVC or coil stock under the flat bar to avoid scratching the finish, gently lift the plank up about ¼ in. at each blind nail location, and use the Malco tool or recip saw to cut the nails. Don’t pry too much or you’ll break the top edge of the overlying plank. As you cut the nails, have a helper hold one end of the plank so you can control its removal and be careful sliding the plank downward so the cut-off nails don’t scratch the plank beneath.

    With the first plank out of the way, most of the nails holding the next plank down are exposed. Pull the exposed nails using the flat bar method: insert the flat bar between the plank and the wall sheathing at the nail location and pry against the wall; once the nail is broken free and raised 1/4 in., push the top of the plank back against the wall so the nail head is proud, and finish pulling the nail with the flat bar. Cut any blind nails that remain before removing the plank.

    According to recent reports, continue working down, removing planks left and right as close to the taped-out area as possible. Remove the cut nails from the planks so they don’t scratch the siding during handling, and label the planks so you can reinstall them in the same locations.

    After you make your wall repair, install a latest piece of water-resistive barrier (WRB) taped along its perimeter to the existing WRB and tuck its top under the existing WRB to shed water. Then reinstall the planks in reverse sequence. I install new nails in the old holes, using ring-shank nails with a slightly larger diameter than the originals for a secure grip. At the ends of planks where they slide beneath an overlying course, you’ll have to face-nail. Make sure the nail penetrates through the overlap at the underlying and overlying planks near where the blind nail used to be.

    According to recent reports, work your way up the wall until you reach the last plank that will slip beneath the existing plank at the top of the repaired area, then face-nail the last reinstalled plank. Face nails can be left exposed and touched up with color-matching paint, but they will be noticeable compared to the blind-nailed siding on the rest of the wall. You can somewhat hide the heads by countersinking them: Make recesses with a drill-mounted countersink and then putty and paint the heads so they’re less obvious. Don’t try hammering the nail heads below the siding surface because you’ll break the fiber cement and the nails won’t hold well.

    • Industry observers note that I’m about to build a house on the coast in Charleston, S.C.
    • Sources indicate that it’s wise to consider inward vapor drive in humid climates like Charleston.
    • Industry observers note that there are a few ways to prevent this.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that I’m about to build a house on the coast in Charleston, S.C. (Climate Zone 3A). It’s elevated on wood pilings and the space under the house is open to the outdoors, enclosed only with louvered panels between the pilings. I have most of the enclosure details nailed down, but I haven’t determined the best way to air-seal and insulate the open floor trusses above the pilings. My biggest concern is hot, humid air from below reaching the underside of the air-conditioned subfloor and condensing on the surface. What’s the best strategy to insulate and air-seal the underside of an elevated coastal home?

    Sources indicate that it’s wise to consider inward vapor drive in humid climates like Charleston. When the outdoor dew point is higher than the air-conditioned indoor temperature, there’s going to be a strong moisture drive from the outside toward the home’s interior, which allows water to accumulate in the materials below the flooring. Prolonged wetting can lead to rotted framing, mold problems, and damaged flooring, along with damage to other materials in contact with the floor.

    Industry observers note that there are a few ways to prevent this. One option is to place a vapor-retarding insulation layer—spray foam—right below the subfloor. The outside (bottom) of the foam will be close enough to the outdoor temperature that water won’t condense on the surface, and the foam will substantially block moisture from moving through it. Provided no ductwork is run in the floor, it’s a way to get decent air-sealing, and the cost is reasonable as well.

    That remarked, I don’t like to use spray foam across an entire floor—it’s risky to install and full of questionable chemicals. Another option is to create a conditioned space within the floor system. The challenge is air-sealing around the posts, beams, and structural hardware that hold up the house and the plumbing and electrical lines in this area. Plus, you’ll have to condition the space, which requires additional HVAC work. This can be simple (like adding a supply register and a path back to the house) or pretty involved (running ductwork down walls to reach the underfloor space).

    Recent findings suggest that my third and preferred option is to create an airtight, vapor-retarding layer across the bottom of the floor trusses. A layer of XPS or foil-faced polyiso (don’t use EPS, it’s too vapor-open) across the bottom of the whole floor will help slow vapor drive into the floor system and bring practical benefits like easier air-sealing and a little additional insulation. In Climate Zone 3A, turn to the International Residential Code (IRC) Table 806.5 in the section on roof ventilation for guidance on the R-value needed, since the floor system will have insulation levels comparable to roofs. The table calls for 1/2 in. of rigid insulation. Using the calculation procedure in the table footnotes indicates a higher level (in the 11/2-in. range) might be less risky, assuming you are completely filling a 12-in. to 16-in. floor-truss cavity with blown-in cellulose or fiberglass, which will be more than the code-required R-38 when the table was developed. Cover the foam board with fiberglass-faced drywall sheathing or plywood. Air-­sealing will still be complex given the elevated construction, and attention will need to be paid to the rim joist/perimeter (spray foam works in this area, as shown in the drawing). But, this system would really slow vapor movement throughout the floor system.

    The Best Bench Vises of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4465 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila
