    We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    According to recent reports, during a power outage, a generator that runs on gasoline can provide enough juice to keep your lights on, your groceries from spoiling, and your fans spinning. Set up a portable unit outside your home, and connect appliances inside to its numerous outlets via extension cords. Exactly how many appliances it’ll power at once depends on the wattage that generator can handle.

    Industry observers note that while a portable generator might cost several hundred or even thousands of dollars depending on size and model, when compared to a standby generator, which would kick on automatically to power your home, it’s certainly less expensive. Plus, you may not need a professional electrician to install a portable generator, and you can easily take the unit with you should you move. All that stated, proper operation of the machine is crucial to ensure the safety of your family and your community.

    Before you start up a portable generator, bear in mind these two essential considerations:.

    WEN’s 5600-watt generator has a push-button start and is powerful enough to run household essentials; noise level is about 88 dB. Read the review.

    Because portable gas generators emit carbon monoxide while they’re running and for some time afterward, positioning the generator properly and practicing careful carbon monoxide safety is critical.

    Before you start up the generator, check the fuel gauge and fill the tank with gasoline as needed. (Make sure the generator is on a level surface to get an accurate reading on the fuel gauge.) If you need to add fuel, consult the owner’s manual for fuel requirements.

    In a recent development, next, check the oil level, which is like checking the oil in your car. Locate the oil dipstick (often below a removable maintenance panel). Pull out the dipstick, wipe it off, and then re-insert it. Carefully pull the dipstick straight out once more, then look to see if the oil on the stick falls between the lower and upper limit marks imprinted on the dipstick. Add or change the oil if necessary, referring to your owner’s manual for how to add, what kind to use, and how frequently it needs to be changed.

    Industry observers note that before plugging in, ensure that you won’t overload the generator by connecting more appliances and lights than it is rated to handle. Add up the starting and running wattage of the appliances you want to power simultaneously; refer to their respective user manuals or check the backs or sides of the machines to find this information. The total number should not exceed the wattage limitations of your generator. Check your user’s manual if you’re unsure of how many watts of power your generator can handle. Stagger the use of appliances if necessary to prevent overloading the generator.

    Follow your user manual for instructions on turning on the machine. You typically will need to turn the circuit breaker off and turn the fuel valve on before starting it up. Give the machine a few minutes to warm up, then flip the circuit breaker on.

    It has been revealed that use long, heavy-duty extension cords made for outdoor use to connect appliances to the generator one by one so as not to overload it. Examine cords before use to ensure they are in good condition with no rips or tears. The cord’s wattage rating should be greater than the wattage of what you’ve plugged into it.

    In a recent development, to shut down the generator, turn off or disconnect the appliances plugged into it. Then refer to your user’s manual to power down the generator—typically you’ll need to turn the circuit breaker, engine switch, and fuel valve to the “off” position.

    According to recent reports, wait until the generator is completely cooled down before storing it once power is restored. If you don’t anticipate needing it again for more than a month, drain the fuel and carburetor. Leaving old fuel can damage the generator’s internal parts. Refer to your owner’s manual for storage instructions.

    When running a portable generator, safety is the name of the game. Keep these tips in mind before, during, and after use.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Sources indicate that what makes a yard an eyesore?
    • The good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.

    Sources indicate that what makes a yard an eyesore? It depends on who you ask. Like personal style and hygiene, everyone has different rules when it comes to yard upkeep and design. One person’s cherished garden gnomes might be another’s idea of tacky kitsch. Lawn decor might be a matter of taste, but neglected maintenance like a broken fence or rotting RV in the yard are harder to overlook.

    The good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors. Ahead, find some of the most controversial yard eyesores, with a reminder that curb appeal is always subjective.

    It has been revealed that unmowed grass and overgrown weeds make a yard look neglected and can rapidly crossover into eyesore territory. But that doesn’t mean everyone’s yard has to look perfectly manicured or exactly the same, either. “A yard that is basic is not a problem as long as it is well kept,” real estate broker Erik Leland notes. “You could choose a meadow-style yard or a pollinator garden as long as it is intentional with defined paths and maintained edges.”.

    According to recent reports, vibrant, healthy trees and shrubs add to a home’s curb appeal, but neglected, overgrown or dead ones can quickly tank it. Even if the rest of the yard is well-maintained, lifeless hedges and trees make it look like an eyesore. “Dead shrubs may appear minor. However, they create a larger perception problem if the property owner is not maintaining something minor, like dead shrubs,” real estate agent Ben Mizes says.

    According to recent reports, broken or unused bulky items like patio furniture, piles of lumber, old furniture or broken lawn equipment can quickly pile up in the yard and become an eyesore. Difficult to dispose of, these items can overwhelm homeowners. “When you see clutter and junk in or around a home, it can create stress and uneasiness, even for neighbors,” Realtor Dell Jeanty says. “Keeping the yard organized can make the property and the entire street feel cleaner and more welcoming.”.

    Recent findings suggest that fences can add to a home’s curb appeal and value, but a neglected one is just a yard eyesore. Broken, rotting and leaning fences drag down a property’s appeal and give the impression it’s not cared for. However, “a fence does not have to be fresh to look good,” real estate expert Cameron Walker says. “Old fences can be painted, and neglected and damaged fences can be repaired to make a good first impression.”.

    It has been revealed that adding statues and garden gnomes to your yard is a personal choice that not everyone will enjoy. What makes you smile may make your neighbor scratch their head. But, even if you are a fan, it is possible to have too much of a good thing. “The right amount of decorations can give personality to a yard and make it inviting, but too many can give a cluttered appearance,” Walker claims. “Decorations should be placed to give ample space to display the landscaping.”.

    Recent findings suggest that while low-maintenance artificial turf is appealing, it can look like an eyesore if not done correctly. Low-quality material and shoddy installation methods result in uneven seams and a cheap aesthetic. “One of the major problems is if it appears as if the grass has been glued to the ground,” Mizes states. But, even when done right, some people just don’t like the look of fake turf. It comes down to personal preference.

    A few carefully placed ornaments can give a yard character, but too many create an eyesore of visual clutter. “A property can lose appeal with an overabundance of various garden ornaments competing for focal points throughout the landscape,” Mizes says. “[But] a collection within a defined area of the landscape can be better appreciated.” Just know that your vision of a beautiful yard might look like a flea market to your neighbor.

    Recent findings suggest that “There’s nothing wrong with having garbage and recycling bins in the front yard during pick-up day, but leaving them lined up in front of the house all week doesn’t look great and robs the home of its curb appeal,” Jeanty notes. “Tucking them beside the house or behind a small screen keeps the yard looking cleaner.” On the other hand, some folks just don’t see what the big deal is about hiding trash cans and that’s okay, too.

    In a recent development, broken down cars, ATVs or campers strewn in a yard qualify as a yard eyesore in most people’s eyes. Mice settle in, lawn and weeds grow around it and your property can start to resemble a junk yard. It knocks down your curb appeal and impacts your home’s value and your neighbor’s, too. A non-working vehicle doesn’t automatically constitute an eyesore, though, if it’s stored intentionally and preferably out of sight.

    While they may spread holiday cheer, not everyone cares for inflatable yard decorations. Where some see whimsy, others see tacky. No matter which side you’re on, most would agree that when deflated during the day, inflatables turn into a yard eyesore. “They just look like piles of plastic in your yard,” Leland notes. Additionally, too many inflatables can be fun or make a yard look disorganized and cluttered, depending on your take.

    Recent findings suggest that “A derelict shed or rotting play structure is sure to give a bad impression,” Leland says. “If it’s not worth repairing, remove it. An empty space is the better choice.” When I moved into my current home, one of the first things we did was remove a large gazebo that was long past its prime. Our latest neighbors all came by and thanked us for removing the neighborhood eyesore.

    Recent findings suggest that kitschy lawn ornaments like plastic flamingos could elicit an eye roll from a neighbor, but perhaps not. “A couple of plastic flamingos can be funny and add personality to a yard, so I wouldn’t automatically call them an eyesore,” Jeanty states. “But when there are twenty of them with mismatched colors competing with signs, flags and other decorations, it becomes a little overwhelming.” Thoughtfully incorporate your outdoor decor into the landscape for a more tasteful display.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that some excerpts from the long opinion by Judge Thomas Thrash (N.D. Ga.) yesterday in Winer v. Mohammad:.

    This action arises out of alleged defamatory statements that Defendant Umaymah Mohammad, a student at the Emory University School of Medicine, made about Plaintiff Joshua Winer, a physician and professor at Emory. Mohammad, who is Palestinian, sent an email to the entire School of Medicine student and faculty body on January 17, 2024, in which the Plaintiff alleges she "praised terrorism against Israel, expressed her hatred towards Israel and the United States, and stated that Israel, the United States, and Emory are perpetrating a genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.".

    In a recent development, nearly two months later, in March 2024, the Plaintiff published an op-ed piece in an Israeli news publication sharing his decision to travel to Israel to volunteer as a physician in the Israeli Defense Force ("IDF") following the October 7th Hamas attack on Israel. The Plaintiff identifies as Jewish and maintains dual American and Israeli citizenship. He is a surgical oncologist at Emory Winship Cancer Institute, a professor in the Department of Surgery, Division of Surgical Oncology at the School of Medicine, and serves as the School of Medicine Surgical Clerkship Director.

    In April 2024, Mohammad participated in an interview for a news organization called Democracy Now!. In the interview, Mohammad was asked about the email she sent and was asked to explain the importance of the issue to her. As part of her response, Mohammad referenced Winer by stating that.

    one of the professors of medicine we have at Emory recently went to serve as a volunteer medic in the Israeli Offense Force [sic] and recently came back. This man participated in aiding and abetting a genocide, in aiding and abetting the destruction of the healthcare system in Gaza and the murder of over 400 healthcare workers, and is now back at Emory so-called teaching medical students and residents how to take care of patients.

    Recent findings suggest that mohammad was ultimately suspended from the School of Medicine for one year based on her comments in the Democracy Now! interview. In November 2024, Mohammad participated in a podcast hosted by the International Union of Scientists in which she made similar statements about the Plaintiff. In January 2025, she made more statements about the Plaintiff's IDF service in the online publication Mondoweiss. In the Mondoweiss piece, Mohammad claimed that the Plaintiff "believe[d] in the legitimacy of apartheid, and that some human lives are not as notable as others.".

    Sources indicate that at the end of the piece, she provided a link to a social media post by Defendants National Students for Justice in Palestine ("NSJP") and Doctors Against Genocide ("DAG"), which ultimately led to a campaign on the website of Action Network that "contained additional false statements about Plaintiff and identified him by name." NSJP and DAG also published posts on Instagram regarding the Action Network campaign, which directly quoted Mohammad's Democracy Now! interview. These Defendants made a second Instagram post a few weeks later. The Plaintiff alleges that Defendant WESPAC is NSJP's fiscal sponsor and, therefore, "knowingly funded and facilitated NSJP's coordinated efforts to vilify Plaintiff and pressure Emory to discipline [him].".

    In February 2025, Defendant CAIR Georgia held a press conference on the subject of Mohammad's suspension, during which she made the following statement:.

    [Emory] disciplined me for exposing Emory's complicity in the destruction of Gaza in an interview where I mentioned an unnamed physician who served in the military, actively engaged in the genocidal campaign against the Palestinian people, my people … I cannot learn from a physician who might have fired one of the 355 bullets that landed in 6 year old Hind Rajab's body. Or who might have helped make the decision to bomb one of the hospitals in Gaza. Or who might have celebrated the murder of our communities on the rubble still wet with Palestinian blood. A doctor who cannot see Palestinians as human beings will return to Atlanta to offer the same disposability to black and brown patients at home.

    CAIR Georgia, along with CAIR Foundation Inc. ("CAIR Foundation"), also issued a press release with a link to Mohammad's Democracy Now! interview and rebroadcasted this speech on its Instagram account on February 11, 2025. In this post, (the "IG Post"), CAIR Georgia also replied to comments by providing a link to a previously circulated email template and phone script that identified the Plaintiff by name and called for Emory to investigate him and/or terminate his employment.

    Sources indicate that mohammad's statements were later broadcasted and published by television stations and news outlets. Defendant Ibrahim Jouja was the President of Emory SJP when it shared NSJP and DAG's posts on the Emory SJP Instagram account, and also made or collaborated on similar posts sharing the Democracy Now! interview and identifying the Plaintiff "as a physician with military combat experience against Palestinians." Defendant Rupa Marya works with Mohammad as a cofounder of DAG and, the Plaintiff alleges, she has "frequently identified Plaintiff by name and used her social media platforms to spread harmful and reputationally damaging statements about him," including blaming him for the termination of a Palestinian professor at Emory School of Medicine and accusing him of participating in a genocide….

    In a recent development, the court allowed plaintiff's federal claim for conspiracy to interfere with civil rights (42 U.S.C. § 1985) to go forward:.

    Section 1985(3) "created a cause of action against private individuals who, among other things, undertake conspiracies for the purpose of depriving, either directly or indirectly, any person or class of persons of the equal protection of the laws, or of equal privileges and immunities under the laws." "That § 1985(3) reaches private action does not, however, mean that it was intended to apply to all tortious, conspiratorial interferences with the rights of others." ….

    It has been revealed that the Plaintiff hinges [the remaining part of] his § 1985(3) claim on the alleged violations of his rights under … Title VI. The Eleventh Circuit does not appear to have addressed whether a violation of Title VI is enforceable against a private conspirator under § 1985(3), so for the reasons the Court expressed in its prior orders, the Court presumes that it is. To state a claim under § 1985(3), a plaintiff must establish that the defendant has.

    (1) conspired or gone in disguise on the highway or on the premises of another, (2) for the purpose of depriving, either directly or indirectly, any person or class of persons of the equal protection of the laws, or of equal privileges and immunities under the laws, (3) taken or caused an action to be taken in furtherance of the conspiracy's object, and (4) injured an individual's person or property or deprived her of exercising any right or privilege of a United States citizen.

    Title VI provides that no one shall "be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance" on the ground of his "race, color, or national origin." To state a claim under § 2000d, a plaintiff must only allege that the defendant receives federal funds, that it discriminated against the plaintiff on the basis of race, color, or national origin, and that it did so in the course of a federally funded program….

    [Plaintiff asserts] a § 1985(3) claim based on a conspiracy to induce Emory to violate his Title VI rights. And for purposes of a motion to a dismiss, he has stated such a claim as to the CAIR Foundation theory. The Plaintiff alleges that CAIR Foundation receives federal funding, making § 2000d enforceable against it. More specifically, he alleges that CAIR Foundation received federal funding, that it conspired with the other defendants, including Mohammad and Jouja, to subject him to discrimination based on his race and national origin by posting the IG Posts at glitch, which he alleges were defamatory and filled with false accusations, and that this discrimination was carried out "in the administration of CAIR Foundation's program or activities receiving Federal financial assistance." The Plaintiff also identifies the specific actions he alleges the Defendants took in furtherance of the conspiracy, including the statements Mohammad made that Jouja is allegedly responsible for as president of Emory SJP. At this early stage, these allegations satisfy the elements of a § 1985(3) claim predicated on a Title VI violation.

    Sources indicate that whether this claim can withstand summary judgment is a question for another day. Accordingly, the Defendants' Motion to Dismiss is denied as to this argument.

    In the process, the court also held that plaintiff had adequately alleged the "protected class" element of § 1985(3), by alleging that he was targeted for his national origin:.

    In a recent development, the Defendants next argue that the Plaintiff unfairly conflates anti-Zionism with antisemitism in order to "place an entire area of First Amendment-protected political, legal and ethical discussion off limits." … The Defendants essentially argue that because Zionism is (in their view) solely a political philosophy, the Plaintiff has actually alleged that their actions were not truly motivated by his Jewish identity but instead by their opposition to Zionism and serving in the IDF. But taking that view would require the Court to construe the Plaintiff's allegations narrowly and in their favor, which it cannot do at this stage.

    What the Plaintiff actually alleges, if construed in his favor—and what the Court must accept as true at this stage—is that his military service resulted from a "sense of duty to serve the Jewish homeland, which is integral to his racial identity as a Jew" ["racial" is here used in the historical sense that included what we would now call "ethnicity," consistent with the Court's caselaw on § 1985 and related statutes -EV] and that his association with Zionism is also "an integral part of Jewish identity for a very significant number of Jews." In essence, the Plaintiff alleges that his military service and association with Zionism are markers of his own personal Jewish identity, and that his Jewish heritage as an Israeli national is a protected class.

    Recent findings suggest that critical to this interpretation is the Plaintiff's allegations that his IDF service was tied to the duty he felt based on his nationality and the significance of Zionism in Jewish culture. These allegations suffice at this stage to demonstrate that a discriminatory animus based on a protected class—the Plaintiff's national origin—motivated the Defendants' actions, not mere political differences.

    And the court concluded that plaintiff had adequately alleged that defendants' speech fell within the First Amendment exception for defamation. It concluded that plaintiff had adequately alleged that he wasn't a limited purpose public figure, despite his op-ed. And the court concluded that plaintiff had adequately alleged that the statements about him contained false factual assertions:.

    Plaintiff asserts that parts of Mohammad's statement in the Democracy Now! interview are demonstrably false, including her statements that the Plaintiff "aid[ed and abett[ed] a genocide" and "aid[ed] and abett[ed] the destruction of the healthcare system in Gaza." Regardless of whether these statements express political opinion, the statements could reasonably "imply defamatory facts about the plaintiff that are capable of being proved false" when the facts are construed in the Plaintiff's favor[.] This is because Mohammad's statements—that the Plaintiff alleges Jouja is responsible for reposting as president of Emory SJP, along with supportive commentary—imply that the Plaintiff actively participated in combat operations during his service in the IDF, but the Plaintiff pled that he served.

    Recent findings suggest that solely in his capacity as a physician, providing medical care to wounded soldiers. His involvement in combat was limited to situations in which his unit came under direct attack … Mohammad had no factual basis to claim that Plaintiff participated in or approved the bombing of hospitals in Gaza [or] celebrated the killing of Palestinians.

    The Court agrees with the Defendants' position that characterizing the Israel-Hamas war as a genocide is likely an inactionable opinion because it reflects a "subjective assessment, as to which reasonable minds could differ, [and which] cannot be proved false." But the statements at concern here go further and allege personal combat participation in the alleged genocide—a fact which the Plaintiff could prove at a later stage is false. At this stage, his allegations about his role are enough to satisfy the "false and defamatory statement" element of his defamation per se claim and the falsity element of his false light claim.

    The same is true of part of Mohammad's statement during the press conference, in which she stated that.

    [h]aving a physician faculty member who participated in a military convicted of committing genocide against Palestinians makes me feel unsafe. It makes black and brown medical students feel unsafe. It makes black and brown and indigenous patients feel unsafe. I cannot learn from a physician who might have fired one of the 355 bullets that landed in 6 year old Hind Rajab's body. Or who might have helped make the decision to bomb one of the hospitals in Gaza … a doctor who cannot see Palestinians as human beings will return to Atlanta to offer the same disposability to black and brown patients at home.

    It has been revealed that there are parts of the statement that express Mohammad's opinion, such as the part that the Plaintiff's military service makes her, and "black and brown medical students," feel unsafe. This is a subjective assessment that cannot be proved false, so this part of the statement is not actionable. But the part of the statement that suggests the Plaintiff might have been involved in combat decisions or actions and accuses him of not "see[ing] Palestinians as human beings" and offering "the same disposability to black and brown patients" at Emory certainly implies that the Plaintiff engaged in combat operations while serving in the IDF and that patients of certain races are therefore not safe in his care.

    The same is true of the statement in Emory SJP's March 28, 2025 collaborative IG Post that described the Plaintiff as "a physician with military combat experience against Palestinians." The Plaintiff has alleged counter-facts that, if accepted as true, prove these portions of the statements false, so the Plaintiff states a claim as to these portions of the press conference statement and the March 28 Emory SJP IG Post.

    In a recent development, for these reasons, the Court will dismiss the portion of the Plaintiff's defamation and false light claims predicated on the opinion portions of the statements identified above. The Court will deny the Defendants' Motion to Dismiss as to the remainder of their First Amendment and opinion-based arguments….

    Particulate matter—including tiny airborne particles like pollen, smoke, soot, and other debris—is one of the most common indoor air pollutants, says Dr. Jaspreet Dhau, an expert on indoor air quality and purification and vice president of research and development at Molekule in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida. “Fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, which is a particle measuring 2.5 microns [micrometers] or smaller, is a concern because it can travel deep into the respiratory system,” says Dhau. Common sources include cooking, burning candles, using a fireplace, vacuuming, and even opening windows when outdoor pollution levels are high.

    VOCs are gases released by certain household products and materials such as paint, solvents, flooring, furniture, adhesives, cleaning supplies, air fresheners, and personal care products. “VOC levels may be higher during and after a home renovation, when new furniture is brought into a home, or when products containing chemical ingredients are used without adequate ventilation,” says Dhau. For example, certain pressed wood furniture and building materials can release formaldehyde, he explains.

    Recent findings suggest that carbon monoxide (CO) is a combustion byproduct, a pollutant released when something burns. “In a typical home, sources can include gas stoves, fireplaces, wood-burning stoves, furnaces, water heaters, candles, and tobacco products,” says Dhau. “Carbon monoxide is especially dangerous because it’s colorless and odorless, making it difficult to detect without a working CO alarm.”.

    It has been revealed that biological contaminants such as dust mites and pet dander are airborne pollutants that originate from living organisms, claims Dhau. “Dust mites are a frequent problem and tend to collect in mattresses, carpets, upholstered furniture, and bedding. They can enter homes through open windows, pets, clothing, and HVAC systems,” he explains. Signs you might have a problem include frequent dust buildup on surfaces, allergy symptoms, excess pet hair and dander, and dust accumulating around air vents, adds Bill Myers, indoor air quality expert and group manager for technical sales at Panasonic Eco Systems North America.

    I thought I'd pass along this tribute, which I thought was moving and apt:.

    Dinner with Judge Richard Posner.

    Recent findings suggest that twenty years ago, I was elevated to chair the antitrust section of the State Bar of Arizona, and I needed a headliner to pack the room for my first event. Who in the world of antitrust could draw interest outside that world? The answer was obvious: the closest thing antitrust has to a rock star, Judge Richard Posner.

    So I cold-emailed Judge Posner an invitation to address judges, lawyers and law students in Tempe. I doubted he would reply, but he did, quickly. He would be happy to come—under one condition. I told him to name it.

    Recent findings suggest that no antitrust law. Anything but antitrust law.

    I agreed, of course. He could have lectured on gardening for all I cared.

    According to recent reports, we all have our favorite jurists, past and present. Until last week, Judge Posner was my favorite living one. He died at 87. His writing is the reason I became an antitrust lawyer.

    Thirty years in the law, and I still turn to one trusted source when an problem is opaque or abstract. I run a quick Westlaw search for Judge Posner's take, and the fog lifts.

    Judge Posner wrote more than 3,300 judicial opinions, and he wrote them to be understood. He embodied what Judge Learned Hand preached nearly a century ago: "The language of law must not be foreign to the ears of those who are to obey it." Posner wrote for the people.

    It has been revealed that he turned abstract ideas into concrete images. Consider his advice to lawyers who ignored the law that cut against them: "The ostrich is a noble animal, but not a proper model for an appellate advocate." I'm not endorsing the tone, but the point slugs you in the jaw.

    Sources indicate that posner made hard things look easy, and he worked hard at it. He confessed to going through up to 20 drafts to give his opinions "a casual, colloquial, and spontaneous appearance." As he put it, "I admit to hypocrisy in working so hard to give the appearance of effortlessness!".

    Judge Posner kept his promise and came to Arizona to speak on judicial independence, not antitrust. That night I hosted him for dinner at El Chorro, nestled at the base of Camelback and Mummy mountains.

    It has been revealed that I was scared. What would I say to Richard Posner for two hours? Convinced I could not carry the conversation alone, I recruited reinforcements, including the Chief Justice of the Arizona Supreme Court and a neurosurgeon.

    According to recent reports, I opened with a safe question. Had anyone seen any good movies lately?

    Posner went first. The last movie he had seen in a theater was Superman. In 1978. Of course. Of course that was the last movie he saw. He did not have time for those trifling pursuits.

    Sources indicate that but then he leaned in. He and his wife had recently bought the first three seasons of 24 on DVD. Each episode, he marveled, captured one hour in a single day in the life of the protagonist, a man named Jack Bauer. A clock even appeared in the lower left-hand corner of the screen so viewers could watch the minutes tick by in real time. Posner narrated his favorite scenes as Bauer landed in one jam after another and always found a way out.

    In a recent development, I have told that story to my law clerks for years. Posner described 24 with the passion and precision he brought to his opinions.

    Posner was an independent thinker who questioned what everyone else assumed, including his own views. He was a founder of the law and economics movement, building much of it with his longtime friend and collaborator, the economist William Landes.

    Recent findings suggest that posner moved antitrust from the boardroom to the checkout line. He asked whether the alleged anticompetitive conduct created efficiencies and raised or lowered prices for consumers. Courts had not always asked. The Chicago School has largely guided courts and regulators since the Reagan years.

    I wrote one book. Posner wrote more than 50, ranging from Law and Literature to Reflections on Judging, all while carrying a full caseload. A 2000 study by Fred Shapiro ranked him the most cited legal scholar of the second half of the twentieth century.

    Recent findings suggest that posner's opinions will lift the fog for generations of advocates. A reporter once asked him how law schools could improve legal writing. He noted he would have first-year students read Holmes, Learned Hand and Robert Jackson, then try to write with their clarity. Posner is on that list. Law schools should teach his writing.

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Recent findings suggest that your riding lawnmower can do double duty this winter by adding a snow plow. Here’s what you need to know before adding a plow to your riding mower.

    Snow is considered a “four-letter” word in our home. Living in the northeast, right in the middle of the so called “I-95” corridor, we usually average 20 inches of snow a year. Even with my trusted 26-inch two-stage snow blower and my newest gadget, an 18 volt snow shovel, clearing the driveway and sidewalk can quickly turn into a significant time consuming and dangerous job. If you already own a riding mower (different from a lawn or garden tractor), you may wonder if you can add a snow plow to turn it into a useful piece of year-round equipment.

    Recent findings suggest that the short answer is “yes, maybe,” said David Bodzioch, certified Small Engine and Automotive Technology Instructor. Snow (plow) blades are available for certain riding mowers. However, Bodzioch cautioned, “attaching a blade doesn’t necessarily make your mower ready to clean a snow-covered driveway.”.

    Accessory compatibility, traction, mower size as well as the amount and type of snow you typically need to move will determine if you can, or should, add a plow blade to your riding lawnmower. Before investing in a plow, you need to understand what your mower can realistically handle. As well as determining what accessories you might need. Here’s what our experts have to say about turning a riding mower into a snow plow.

    Industry observers note that “Yes, many riding lawnmowers can be equipped with a front-mounted snow blade,” noted certified Small Engine instructor Jeffrey Cesari. “Even if aftermarket compatible attachments are available, you should use the manufacturer’s approved attachments,” added Cesari. “Adding a plow blade on small tractors requires a set of rear wheel chains and a counterweight for balance,” added Cesari.

    For example, John Deere sells a front blade package (as well as snow throwers) designed for specific riding lawnmowers. A John Deer 19 horsepower or better twin-cylinder engine units position the driver closer to the engine for better balance.

    What Do You Need to Turn a Riding Lawnmower Into a Snow Plow?

    Industry observers note that “At minimum, you’ll need a snow blade and direct-fit mounting hardware designed to fit your particular make and model mower,” said Bodzioch. Tire chains and weights should also be considered when operating snow-clearing equipment. According to Troy-Bilt, makers of outdoor power equipment, “Depending on the riding lawnmower mower and snow conditions, the mower will benefit from the added traction that chains and weights provide” when removing snow.

    According to recent reports, “It depends on whether your mower simply requires a blade, or the added cost of mounting hardware, weights and tire chains,” mentioned Cesari. An add on blade can cost as little as $120 for 22 to 32 inch width universal riding mower plow kit, to over $1400 for a complete John Deere 46 inch front blade snow plow package that includes an adjustable three-position blade height and angle setting you can change from the driver’s seat. Look for heavy-gauge steel blades that are height-adjustable and have the ability to reposition the shave plate for longer life.

    In a recent development, the biggest advantage is getting year-round use from expensive equipment you already own. Plus, eliminating the need for another piece of snow-removal equipment that sits unused for nine or ten months out of the year.

    “You’ll probably need to buy and install several accessories and that can be expensive,” stated Bodzioch. You should also check how difficult it is swapping out the snow blade and grass cutting mower deck. He added that “you also want check if your mower and blade combination are right for your type [concrete, blacktop, etc.] driveway.”.

    Yes, it can be, and should be, as long as your mower is approved for the attachment, is well-maintained and in good working condition. Following the manufacturer’s operating, maintenance guides and safety instructions is mandatory for safe and efficient operation; the same as when using any other piece of outdoor power equipment.

    Bodzioch said, “Proper traction is especially vital when driving on ice and snow, or on snow-covered grass or soil.” But Cesari also notes that “you need to be aware of frame structure and that adding a snow plow can cause frame damage, transmission wear and belt fatigue on small home riding mowers.” Cesari said plowing up to five inches should be safe. Always be cautious and use common sense if your mower is struggling while removing any amount of snow.

    Industry observers note that it depends. It may only make sense if you already own a compatible mower. However, having room and space to safely store the blade should be a real consideration. Cesari added, “Converting your mower to a plow may require buying expensive attachments or accessories. Consider a standalone snow blower or a lawn/garden tractor if it’s difficult swap out the mower deck and plow.” If you regularly deal with challenging snow conditions, a dedicated snow-removal machine may be the better investment.

    In a recent development, it depends on how you use the word. While “riding mower” and “lawn tractor” are often interchangeable, there are key differences between the two pieces of equipment. A riding mower typically means any mower you sit on, including a lawn tractor or zero-turn mower. Nevertheless, a lawn/garden tractor will generally be more expensive and have a larger, sturdier frame. Lawn/garden tractors are designed and built to accept manufacturers’ compatible direct-fit attachments and accessories.

He also won the prestigious Harbor Freight Tools for Schools Award, obtained a masters equivalence in industrial education. Jef is also a certified PennDoT safety inspector and instructor. Jeff also earned five industry recognized certifications, including 4-cycle and 2-cycle engines, electrical, compact diesel and mechanical systems through the Equipment and Engine Training Council (EETC).     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I thought I'd serialize my newly introduced Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the first Part:.

    In certain areas, First Amendment precedent turns out to be quite consistent with original meaning—even though the Court hasn't squarely discussed historical evidence in any detail. This might be a fortunate accident, or perhaps a random coincidence in the policy judgments of the modern Court and the Framing generation. But I expect that some at least stems from a phenomenon that Justice Scalia discussed in McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Commission (1995): "Principles of liberty fundamental enough to have been embodied within constitutional guarantees are not readily erased from the Nation's consciousness. A governmental practice that has become general throughout the United States, and particularly one that has the validation of long, accepted usage, bears a strong presumption of constitutionality.".

    Sources indicate that in some situations, this observation may not be accurate. But in others, there really does appear to be a longstanding constitutional understanding that has become so much part of the law that a court that simply follows doctrine will incorporate original meaning. Let me offer three examples.

    A. "The Liberty of the Press Is Not Confined to Newspapers and Periodicals".

    It has been revealed that the Supreme Court has generally held that the First Amendment equally protects all who speak to the public, whether they are professional media (e.g., newspaper publishers or reporters) or nonprofessionals (e.g., leafletters). In this respect, it has treated "the freedom … of the press" as protecting the press as technology—the use of the printing press and its technological heirs—rather than the press as industry, in the sense of people whose daily job is writing for the public.

    It has been revealed that now the original articulation of this position in the Supreme Court came in Lovell v. City of Griffin (1938), with little historical analysis:.

    Industry observers note that the liberty of the press is not confined to newspapers and periodicals. It necessarily embraces pamphlets and leaflets. These indeed have been historic weapons in the defense of liberty, as the pamphlets of Thomas Paine and others in our own history abundantly attest. The press in its historic connotation comprehends every sort of publication which affords a vehicle of information and opinion.

    And this is so even though the Court had shown an interest in Framing-era history. Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson (1931) discussed that history in striking down an injunction against the operation of a "scandalous" newspaper. Grosjean v. American Press Co. (1936) discussed history in considerably more detail in holding unconstitutional a selective tax on certain newspapers.

    Recent findings suggest that more recently, Justice Scalia's concurrence in Citizens United v. FEC (2010) offered a bit more historical analysis:.

    According to recent reports, the dissent … interpret[s] the Freedom of the Press Clause to refer to the institutional press (thus demonstrating, according to the dissent, that the Founders "did draw distinctions—explicit distinctions—between types of 'speakers,' or speech outlets or forms"). It is passing strange to interpret the phrase "the freedom of speech, or of the press" to mean, not everyone's right to speak or publish, but rather everyone's right to speak or the institutional press's right to publish. No one thought that is what it meant. Patriot Noah Webster's 1828 dictionary contains, under the word "press," the following entry:.

    "Liberty of the press, in civil policy, is the free right of publishing books, pamphlets or papers without previous restraint; or the unrestrained right which every citizen enjoys of publishing his thoughts and opinions, subject only to punishment for publishing what is pernicious to morals or to the peace of the state.".

    As the Court's opinion describes, our jurisprudence agrees with Noah Webster and contradicts the dissent.

    In a recent development, "The liberty of the press is not confined to newspapers and periodicals. It necessarily embraces pamphlets and leaflets…. The press in its historical connotation comprehends every sort of publication which affords a vehicle of information and opinion.".

    But this is still predominantly a precedential analysis, with one textual argument and one early republican source.

    At the same time, the foundational case in the Court—Lovell—followed 150 years of established practice, to the point that the Court might not have seen the need to do more than just nod to "[t]he press in its historic connotation.".

    As I've laid out elsewhere, Framing-era legal sources, such as cases, treatises, and constitutional provisions, articulated the freedom of the press as extending to everyone, not just to professional newspaper publishers. {See generally Eugene Volokh, Freedom for the Press as an Industry, or for the Press as a Technology? From the Framing to Today, 160 U. Pa. L. Rev. 459 (2012) [hereinafter Volokh, Freedom for the Press]; Eugene Volokh, The Press Clause: Notable, Remembered, and Equally Shared, 5 J. Free Speech L. 659 (2025).} Then, starting in the 1820s, courts began to expressly hold that newspaper printers' and editors' rights were equal to everyone else's. In the following decades, that was repeated in case after case throughout the country. By the time Lovell was decided, the principle was well-established in the precedents, and, to my knowledge, unanimously so. The original meaning had made its way into well-settled doctrine and was then ratified by the Court in Lovell.

    The original meaning also fit with practice, which took place in the shadow of the law but which likely also affected the law. In the Framing era, many influential Americans published their views using the printing press, whether in pamphlets or as submissions to newspapers. It would be odd to think that they would have secured special constitutional rights to the just-emerging category of newspapermen, who were in some measure lower status than they were, while denying the same rights to themselves.

    According to recent reports, and though those newspapers became relatively more influential in the following centuries, a tradition of leafletting and pamphleteering continued. The Court in 1938 could see the media reality as well as media law and naturally view the nonprofessional leafletter as having the same free press rights as a professional newspaper editor.

    The very first case in which the Supreme Court struck down government action as violating constitutional rights of freedom of expression, Stromberg v. California (1931), involved neither the press nor speech in the literal sense. Rather, it involved what one might today call symbolic expression (or expressive conduct)—the display of a red flag as a revolutionary symbol.

    Recent findings suggest that but the opinion never discussed why displaying a flag counted as "speech" or "press." The opinion below similarly assumed that symbolic expression was as protected as verbal expression, and so did the parties' briefs in the Supreme Court. The Court had neither before nor since analyzed whether this result is consistent with the original meaning of the free expression guarantees. {See Eugene Volokh, Symbolic Expression and the Original Meaning of the First Amendment, 97 Geo. L.J. 1057 (2009).}.

    Likewise, the 1920 California Supreme Court decision in Ex parte Hartman (1920) struck down an earlier law banning the possession or display of flags that represented efforts "espous[ing] for the government of … the United States of America … principles or theories of government antagonistic … to the form of the government thereof as now constituted." The court concluded that Americans have "the right to advocate peaceable changes in our Constitution, laws or form of government," and that therefore "an organization peaceably advocating such changes may adopt a flag … signifying its purpose, and that the display or possession of such flag … cannot be made an unlawful act." The court simply assumed that symbolic expression was constitutionally equivalent to verbal expression, without discussing the matter further.

    But while these assumptions weren't backed by any originalist analysis, they appear to have been fully consistent with the Framing-era understanding that symbolic expression, pictorial expression, and verbal expression were generally treated as functionally equivalent. This equivalence was most often drawn with regard to restrictions on expression, such as defamation law. But it was also the view taken in the early republic with regard to constitutional protections for expression.

    It has been revealed that thus, for instance, pre-Revolutionary libel law recognized the category of libel by "pictures, signs, and the like"—meaning through symbols, whether printed or physically displayed—as tantamount to libel by writing. Early American law did the same, extending the same principle to incitement to riot as well. Early treatises drew this equivalence. Early court decisions suggested that pictorial and symbolic expression was potentially protected by free expression guarantees (though subject to the same constitutionally permissible restrictions, such as libel law, as verbal expression).

    To offer a particularly vivid illustration, consider the report of Mezzara's Case (1817), apparently the earliest American case involving nonverbal libel—there, a painting of the plaintiff with donkey's ears. The reporter, a New York lawyer, followed the case with a note hypothesizing what would happen if the painting were an apt commentary on the subject's folly and lack of patriotism. In such a situation, the reporter wrote, "[I]f the painter could show the truth of the matter in evidence, as before described, and that he published and exhibited the picture, 'with good motives and for justifiable ends,' … would he not be justifiable under our statute?".

    The statute the reporter cites—which did allow truth as a defense in libel actions, if the defendant acted with good motives and for justifiable ends—was passed in the wake of the New York court's evenly dividing in People v. Croswell (1804) on whether the freedom of the press mandated that the defense of truth be allowed in libel prosecutions. The statute implemented Chancellor James Kent's view of the constitutional rule, which was also the view championed by Alexander Hamilton (as Croswell's lawyer) in one of the last public acts of his life, and was seen as an key protection for the liberty of the press. And just four years after Mezzara's Case, at the next New York constitutional convention, the statute's provisions were adopted as part of the New York Constitution.

    It has been revealed that the reporter thus saw nothing odd in treating a painting as protected by free expression principles, just as the court saw nothing odd in treating a painting as punishable under libel law principles. Likewise, three-dimensional symbolic expression, such as the raising of a liberty pole, was similarly treated as being potentially constitutionally protected just as pictorial and verbal expression were (though again subject to the possible constitutional limitations imposed on verbal expression).

    This equivalence of symbolic, pictorial, and verbal expression unsurprisingly endured as part of the law—most often discussed as to libel law—throughout the 1800s and early 1900s. The Supreme Court, for instance, mentioned in 1845 that libel was a "species of defamation which is effected by writing or printing, or by pictures and signs," and in 1904 quoted a law enacted by the Philippine Commission that offered the same definition. There had been hundreds of similar holdings from state courts, whether explicating the common law or state statutes (and often including "effigies" alongside pictures and signs). Legal treatises had set forth the same principle.

    According to recent reports, thus, again, when the cases came before the California Supreme Court in 1920 and the U.S. Supreme Court in 1931, it was natural for the courts and the litigants to casually assume that symbolic expression (there using flags) was likewise treated equivalently to verbal expression for purposes of freedom of expression law. What was accepted in the Framing era continued to be accepted, without any felt need for discussion, in the early 1900s. And here too this conclusion was supported by a long tradition of practice as well as doctrine: Symbolic expression (whether through effigies, processions, visual puns, and the like) was commonplace in the Framing era, and flags and other forms of symbols continued to be used the same way into the 1900s.

    Upcoming York Times Co. v. Sullivan's "actual malice" requirement has of course been criticized as contrary to the original meaning of the First Amendment. But some have also criticized the case on the grounds that it improperly imports freedom of expression principles into civil tort liability. Here too the Court has never tried to explain this particular conclusion on originalist grounds. Likewise, none of the briefs in Sullivan made an originalist argument in favor of applying constitutional limitations to common law civil lawsuits.

    According to recent reports, nonetheless, here too this may have stemmed from the longstanding understanding, dating back to the Framing era, that freedom of expression guarantees did indeed potentially apply to civil liability. We see that starting with 1802 and 1806 decisions from the Vermont and South Carolina high courts, rejecting liability in part by citing the state equivalents of the Petition Clause. {See generally Eugene Volokh, Tort Liability and the Original Meaning of the Freedom of Speech, Press, and Petition, 96 Iowa L. Rev. 249 (2010) (discussing this).}  And we see that in other cases from 1799 onwards that reasoned that constitutional protections may apply to civil lawsuits as well as to criminal prosecutions, but that libelous speech was constitutionally unprotected against civil liability as well as against criminal punishment. Early commentators took the same view.

    And here too the early original meaning turned into well-established constitutional tradition. Throughout the 1800s and 1900s, court decisions routinely assumed that constitutional protections could limit civil liability, though subject to the recognition that there was essentially a First Amendment libel exception for civil as well as criminal liability. By the time of Fresh York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964), this position just wasn't particularly controversial, even if the other features of that decision were.

    You Can Now Get a Battery Just for Your Fridge—But Is It Better Than a Generator?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2342 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
    • Power outages are top of mind now more than ever before—and for good reason.
    • Industry observers note that backup power promises comfort and security, which is why so many homes rely on a portable generator or power station.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    Power outages are top of mind now more than ever before—and for good reason. One in four households experience a power outage in a year, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, and 70 percent of those reporting outages were without power for 6 hours or more. These longer outages are not only disruptive; they can also be expensive, considering that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration recommends tossing perishable food kept in the refrigerator after just 4 hours without power.

    Industry observers note that backup power promises comfort and security, which is why so many homes rely on a portable generator or power station. That category has grown from gas-powered generators to multi-fuel units, portable power stations, and whole-home batteries. The newest member of the family? A fridge backup.

    According to recent reports, just in 2026, this upcoming style hard-debuted with models from three industry leaders: Bluetti’s Fridge Power, Jackery’s FridgeGuard, and Backup Core by BioLite. And the consumer response has been powerful. Bluetti’s Kickstarter hit 145 percent of its funding goal in 45 days. Jackery debuted as a Costco exclusive in June and expanded its retail distribution after hearing about customers carrying home multiple units. BioLite has released its Backup in two waves already, each selling out in weeks, and is taking orders now for January shipments. Clearly, homeowners want a backup built just for the fridge. Keep reading to learn more about what sets fridge backups apart and when one beats a generator.

    Fridge-optimized batteries all share three main hallmarks:.

    Think of it like a larger version of the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) that you might use in a home office or with a high-end entertainment center to keep your connected electronics running during a brownout or blackout. A UPS in the home office might offer surge protection and enough battery life to run your computer for another 5 minutes so you can safely shut it down; this fridge-optimized backup can keep your most notable kitchen appliance on for 15 hours or more.

    And while we call them “fridge” backups, the design is actually much more versatile. Plug them in and slip the slim backups easily into any room to keep an important appliance operational for hours: under a bed to power a CPAP machine, behind a bookshelf within cord’s reach of an air purifier, or behind the fish tank to maintain the family pet’s habitat.

    Sources indicate that kickstarter backers for the Backup by BioLite—which first debuted in 2024 on the crowdfunding platform—“got it” immediately. “They understood the problem it was solving, and most questions revolved around understanding additional applications and setups beyond the fridge because the kitchen application was so intuitive,” states Erica Rosen, the VP of Marketing at BioLite and Goal Zero brands. “For example, we got a lot of questions about sump pumps and if Backup could run one during an outage.” (Spoiler alert: It can.).

    Today, homeowners (and renters!) have many options for backup power, each with its own set of pros and cons.

    A standby generator or whole-home battery backup automatically kicks in to keep the essentials—if not the whole home—running during an outage. Each type of backup connects at the electrical panel with a transfer switch. As such, each is a larger investment (read: more expensive) and a permanent installation that requires a licensed electrician. These backups also require forethought about fuel. A standby generator will require a source of liquid propane and/or natural gas, whereas whole-home batteries are often charged from the grid before an event and potentially recharged via solar panels when the grid is down.

    According to recent reports, A portable gas-powered generator is more affordable than a standby option, but should only be run outdoors, which creates some limitations. For starters, you need to be home to turn a portable generator on and connect to your appliance. Then, you’ll need a long, heavy-duty outdoor-rated extension cord to reach the kitchen. These generators operate loudly, emit exhaust fumes, and require you to store enough fuel to be ready for the worst. Assuming you have a good supply, though, you can keep your appliance(s) powered with minimal interruption using a reliable portable generator.

    Sources indicate that A power station brings backup power indoors to power multiple electronics and small appliances. Power stations are the closest comparison. They are safe to use indoors or out and feature similar battery capacities. You can find options in the ballpark of 1 to 2 kWh for similar price points. They can, but may not always be, plugged in 100 percent of the time to act as a UPS. And importantly, they’re often too bulky to leave out next to a refrigerator 24/7.

    It has been revealed that A fridge backup offers instant power backup without a permanent installation. It’s ideal for the consumer who is looking for a user-friendly, set-and-forget setup and a safety net that offers enough power to keep a fridge running for approximately 15 hours while the power is out—longer if additional batteries are connected.

    According to recent reports, “It’s [designed for] someone who wants peace of mind without having to think too much about backup power. Maybe you live somewhere with frequent storms, or you’ve come home after an outage to find everything in your freezer has spoiled,” states Beau Tyrrel, Product Manager at Jackery. “It’s also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”.

    The design is appealing in more ways than one, notes Luna Yan, affiliate marketing manager at Bluetti. A fridge backup solves spatial problems that come with more traditional portable power stations: “Traditional backup power systems are often bulky, making them difficult to accommodate in homes with limited space, particularly in kitchens and apartments.”.

    “When we set out to develop Backup, we knew the world didn’t need another box-format power station. We did a lot of user research and found that there was a meaningful gap between the power stations of the world and expensive whole-home backup solutions, and it was leaving a lot of people out of the resiliency conversation,” Rosen states. “As we explored ways to answer this, it became clear that form factor was going to be a really crucial element: If we wanted something plugged in permanently to enable automatic performance, it needed to be really easy and it could not take up precious living space.”.

    It’s especially useful if you’re away when the power goes out and can’t move the fridge’s plug to a generator. Already plugged into the wall from setup, the backup’s stored power will be usable immediately. Each model’s mobile app shows outage alerts, battery level, and power draw from anywhere.

    “[A fridge backup is] also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”.

    In a recent development, there’s a cost to every power outage. One of the biggest concerns for most homeowners is the spoiled food in a refrigerator after 4 hours without power. “Refrigerators are one of the few appliances in your home that needs to run around the clock,” Tyrrel says. “When the power goes out, you could lose hundreds of dollars in groceries.”.

    A blackout can cost the average American household $117 in spoiled groceries, according to a survey of more than 1,000 Americans by the Texas electric provider Payless Power. One in five homes had it worse, losing more than $200 in groceries during a single outage.

    Sources indicate that using that average, we estimate that a $1,000 fridge backup pays for itself after 10 blackouts—potentially sooner in larger households or homes with especially packed fridges and freezers. For an area that experiences one to two extended blackouts in a year, this investment could earn its keep in as soon as 6 years—and these new backups are rated for 10 or more years of use.

    “Based on customer feedback, refrigerators are among the most important appliances to keep running during a power outage,” Yan says. And for good reason: “Continuous refrigeration helps protect food, medications, and other temperature-sensitive items.”.

    Recent findings suggest that if your utility company offers a Time-of-Use (TOU) electricity pricing plan, any of these fridge backups can help you take advantage of the savings. TOU programs charge different supply rates based on when you use electricity, incentivizing customers to use more electricity when overall demand is low by charging less per kilowatt-hour (kWh) used. These “off-peak hours” vary by plan, but typically are overnight and early morning.

    For the average homeowner, the main way to save on these prepares is to optimize the electricity usage you can schedule: when you charge an electric vehicle, run the dishwasher, and wash or dry a load of laundry. A fridge, of course, runs all day, and an efficient, Energy Star-certified model can use anywhere from 358 kWh for a compact top-freezer unit to 805 kWh per year for a large side-by-side refrigerator. You can’t optimize the always-on appliance without either a whole-home power bank that recharges in an off-peak hour for use during peak times or, now, a fridge backup. In a connected mobile app, consumers specify the best times to charge (off-peak hours) and discharge (peak hours), effectively shifting the fridge’s grid use to cheaper hours.

    Industry observers note that especially now, with rising concern about grid stability and the increasing frequency of natural disaster events that disrupt power, demand for energy backups is high. Each of these energy brands has sold out and replenished stock at least once already this year. So while you may be eager to set up your home with the first available fridge backup, here’s a comprehensive look at unit specs to help find the model best suited to your space and needs.

    In a recent development, bluetti’s fridge backup offers the largest base capacity—nearly double that of Jackery FridgeGuard, and expandable to 8 kWh (second only to BioLite’s 10.5 kWh). Divide the total cost by the capacity, and you’re paying about $470 per kWh, which is the most backup per dollar. One unit can power the typical modern fridge for 21 to 48 hours, and a maximized setup of FridgePower plus three BlueCell battery packs can power your fridge for 4 days. (Run time, of course, depends on the specific refrigerator’s energy consumption and usage conditions.) That makes the slim design even more impressive—though at 43 pounds, it’s a two-person job to wall-mount.

    Sources indicate that the mobile app provides battery levels, outage status, and charging progress, plus a place to choose among four UPS modes: Standard, PV Priority (which prioritizes solar power), TOU (Time-of-Use), and Custom. It even tracks local weather, alerts you when a storm approaches, and switches to fast charging if needed. An optional magnetic display (sold separately) provides at-a-glance information including percentage charged, energy output, and UPS modes—all without opening your phone.

    On paper, the Jackery fridge backup appears to be the unit most specialized for fridge use. It offers up to 15 hours of power in the slimmest profile. One outlet (for the fridge) and a single expansion option make it the least flexible of the three—but if the fridge is all you need, it’s a perfect fit. It’s effective, affordable, lasts up to 16 years, and takes only one person to install the lightweight unit on a wall mount (sold separately). It offers surge protection for your most important household appliance during voltage spikes and enough power to start the fridge.

    One distinction Jackery has over its competition is a choice between instant backup UPS and a delayed start. “Your refrigerator’s compressor needs a little time to recover,” Tyrrel explains. “When it stops, refrigerant pressure remains high on one side of the system. Restarting too quickly makes the motor work harder and briefly draw several times its normal current. Delayed Start gives the compressor a short pause before restarting, helping avoid unnecessary strain when power flickers on and off.”.

    From the moment an outage occurs, Backup Core automatically powers a refrigerator for 15 to 30 hours. At 29 inches long, it’s 5 to 6 inches longer than all of the other units, but rotating it can fit one atop even a fridge and its slim design should still slip behind the appliance on its vertical wall mount.

    Recent findings suggest that given its size and expansion capabilities, it should come as no surprise that Backup Core also includes the most outlets for electronics. Whereas another model includes one or two ports on the unit, the forward-thinking BioLite design provides its own power strip—that’s three more openings for small kitchen appliances or other electronics to easily connect.

    BioLite’s Backup Core is a 1.5 kWh solution, similar to its sister brand Goal Zero Yeti 1500 (6th generation). “However, Backup can expand in 1.5kWh increments with the ‘Extend’ model, and chain up to 10.5kWh of localized capacity,” Rosen explains. That’s even more than the combined 8kWh capacity of the Yeti Pro 4000 and Yeti Pro Tank 4000. So while Backup Core is the priciest of the three, it’s also the only one that can grow into something close to a whole-home battery. Think of it less as a fridge backup and more as the first piece of a backup system.

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Police sirens can sound very different, from a slow wail to a rapid yelp. Here’s why officers switch tones and what drivers should do.

    In a recent development, everyone recognizes an emergency siren. Or do they?

    Officers can choose different tones to make their vehicles easier to notice on busy streets or open roads. Some departments also use certain sounds for special warnings. With electronic siren systems offering several options, drivers might hear multiple tones during a single emergency response.

    Learn what the common sounds mean, why officers switch between them, whether different tones signal different emergencies, and how drivers should react.

    In a recent development, different police siren sounds serve different purposes, but they don’t necessarily indicate specific emergencies. Officers often switch tones based on traffic conditions or to get drivers’ attention. A faster siren doesn’t always mean a more serious emergency.

    The most common police siren sounds include:.

    Modern police vehicles typically use electronic sirens that allow officers to switch between these sounds. Older mechanical sirens use a spinning mechanism to produce a traditional wail.

    Officers also adjust their sirens based on traffic conditions. Faster tones can help get drivers’ attention in heavy traffic, while a slower wail may work on quieter roads. Departments set their own policies for siren use, so there isn’t one standard sound for daytime or nighttime driving.

    Regardless of the siren sound, drivers should respond the same way when an emergency vehicle approaches. Drivers should check their mirrors, signal, and safely pull toward the right side of the road to let the police vehicle pass. They should avoid sudden braking or stopping in an intersection.

    In a recent development, anyone already in an intersection should continue through before pulling over. Drivers waiting at a red light shouldn’t enter the intersection unless an officer directs them to do so. After the police vehicle passes, drivers should check for other emergency vehicles before returning to traffic. Specific rules may vary by state.

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    "Can AI Ace Your Exam? A Penn Law Experiment," by Prof. R. Polk Wagner

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (454 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I report a controlled experiment that ran a frontier large language model through eleven real University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School final exams in Spring 2026 and sent the machine's answers out for blind grading alongside the work of enrolled students.
    • It has been revealed that first, the model is broadly competitive: across the ten exams returned with grades, it passed every one, sat at or above the class median on every one, and reached the top decile on seven.
    • According to recent reports, second, the benefit of supplying course materials is real but concentrated and uneven.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A very interesting preprint; here's the Abstract:.

    I report a controlled experiment that ran a frontier large language model through eleven real University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School final exams in Spring 2026 and sent the machine's answers out for blind grading alongside the work of enrolled students. Each exam was answered twice: once with no course materials in the model's context (the "no-materials" arm, relying on the model's training alone) and once with the course syllabus and an outline supplied (the "with-materials" arm). Three findings emerge.

    It has been revealed that first, the model is broadly competitive: across the ten exams returned with grades, it passed every one, sat at or above the class median on every one, and reached the top decile on seven. On two exams, both scored on an open, non-saturated scale, it outscored every enrolled student.

    According to recent reports, second, the benefit of supplying course materials is real but concentrated and uneven. It is large on multiple-choice components, small to absent on essays, and on one exam the materials helped the machine's multiple-choice score while hurting its essay—so the gain vanishes when the two are averaged into a single number. The subject of the exam matters as much as its format.

    According to recent reports, third, faculty graders detected the AI submissions at a high rate, but mostly through signals that are easy to remove: formatting artifacts, identification-number placement, even a reversed quotation-mark glyph. The detection that survives those fixes is content-based—two independently generated answers that read as though written by the same hand, and a voice that does not match time-pressured student work. One grader was confident enough in detection to decline to grade the AI answers at all.

    I read these results less as a verdict than as a measurement problem: when a model that never took the course can top the curve, it is no longer clear that the time-limited, high-stakes final is measuring what we have long assumed it measures—mastery of this course—rather than fluency in a genre the machine commands. That genre was always a contrivance built for grading, not a faithful model of practice, so the machine's success notes less about lawyering than the headline suggests; but it says a good deal about how much weight the instrument can still bear.

    The urgent ask the experiment surfaces is intentionality: that faculty be clear about what each assessment is meant to measure, and recognize that AI is widening an already-real gap between the law-school exam and the practice it stands in for. The responses will range—from rethinking assessment top to bottom, to narrower adjustments, to simply naming the mismatch and grading with it in view—and reasonable colleagues will differ.
